title: Introduction to OSHA 1926 & Worker Rights
topics: Contractor duty to provide safe working conditions

resources.title: Worker Rights and Protections
resources.description: Official OSHA worker rights and protections guide

test.question: Under 1926.20(a)(1), a contractor or subcontractor may not require a laborer or mechanic to work in surroundings or under conditions that are:
options: Unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to their health or safety
Away from the main project site
test.explanation: No contractor or subcontractor may require a laborer or mechanic to work in surroundings or under working conditions that are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to their health or safety (1926.20(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a subcontractor cannot order a laborer into an unprotected, caving trench to keep the schedule.

test.question: How quickly must an employer report a work-related fatality to OSHA?
test.explanation: A work-related fatality must be reported to OSHA within eight hours after the death (1904.39(a)(1)). In-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must be reported within 24 hours (1904.39(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a worker dies in a trench collapse at 6:00 a.m., so OSHA must be notified by 2:00 p.m.

test.question: Under 1903.11(a), who may request an OSHA inspection by giving notice of an alleged violation?
options: Any employee or representative of employees who believes a violation exists
test.explanation: Any employee or representative of employees who believes a violation of the Act exists in their workplace may request an inspection by notifying the Area Director or a Compliance Safety and Health Officer (1903.11(a)). Job-site scenario: a carpenter who sees missing guardrails on an upper deck can file the request themselves.

test.question: Under 1904.29(a), which forms (or equivalent forms) must an employer that is required to keep injury records use for recordable injuries and illnesses?
options: The workers' compensation first report only
test.explanation: Employers must use the OSHA 300 (Log), 300-A (Summary), and 301 (Incident Report) forms, or equivalents, for recordable injuries and illnesses (1904.29(a)). Each case must be entered within seven calendar days (1904.29(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: a laceration needing stitches is logged on the 300 and documented on a 301 within 7 days.

test.question: Under 1977.12(b)(2), when is an employee who refuses an assigned task protected from discipline?
options: When, with no reasonable alternative, the employee refuses in good faith because a reasonable person would see a real danger of death or serious injury and there is no time to correct it through regular OSHA channels
Any time the employee feels uncomfortable
When the employee prefers a different task
Only after OSHA has issued a citation
test.explanation: A refusal is protected only when the employee, with no reasonable alternative, refuses in good faith; a reasonable person would conclude there is a real danger of death or serious injury; there is not enough time to remove the danger through regular enforcement channels; and, where possible, the employee has asked the employer to correct it (1977.12(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a laborer told to enter a trench whose wall is visibly sloughing, after the foreman refuses to shore it, may refuse.

test.question: Under 1977.15(d)(1), within how many days after an alleged act of retaliation should an employee file a section 11(c) discrimination complaint?
test.explanation: Section 11(c)(2), as stated in 1977.15(d)(1), allows a retaliation complaint to be filed within 30 days after the violation occurs. This limit applies to retaliation complaints, not to hazard complaints asking for an inspection. Job-site scenario: an ironworker fired the day after calling OSHA about missing fall protection has 30 days to file.

test.question: Section 11(c)(1) of the OSH Act, quoted in 1903.11(d), prohibits an employer from:
options: Paying employees who file safety complaints
Allowing OSHA on the job site
Discharging or discriminating against an employee for filing a complaint or exercising any right under the Act
test.explanation: No person may discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for filing a complaint, testifying, or exercising any right afforded by the Act (1903.11(d)). Reporting an injury is also protected (1904.36). Job-site scenario: a foreman cannot cut the hours of a laborer who reported a back injury.

test.question: On a construction project, where must the OSHA notice (poster) required by 1903.2 be posted?
options: In the site trailer's locked office
It may be emailed instead of posted
At the location to which employees report each day
test.explanation: For physically dispersed activities such as construction, the notice must be posted at the location to which employees report each day, in a conspicuous place, and must not be altered, defaced, or covered (1903.2(a)(1); 1903.2(b)). Job-site scenario: post it on the board at the gate where crews sign in each morning.

test.question: A formal employee complaint requesting an inspection under 1903.11(a) must be:
options: Put in writing, describe the grounds with reasonable particularity, and be signed
Supported by at least two witnesses
test.explanation: The notice must be reduced to writing, set forth with reasonable particularity the grounds for the notice, and be signed by the employee or representative. On request, the complainant's name is withheld from the copy given to the employer (1903.11(a)). Job-site scenario: a written, signed complaint describing unguarded floor holes on Level 3 meets the requirement.

test.question: How must employers share annual injury summary data with employees under 1904.32(b)(6)?
options: Post Form 300-A from February 1 to April 30
test.explanation: The annual summary must be posted no later than February 1 of the following year and kept posted until April 30 (1904.32(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: the certified 300-A goes up on the field office posting board by February 1 and stays until April 30.

title: General Safety and Health Provisions
topics: Accident prevention programs and competent-person inspections

resources.title: General Safety Requirements
resources.description: General safety and health provisions standard

test.question: Under 1926.20(b)(2), the employer's accident prevention program must provide for:
options: Weekly inspections by the owner's representative
Frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment by competent persons designated by the employer
test.explanation: Programs must provide for frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment by competent persons the employer designates (1926.20(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: the superintendent assigns a competent person to walk the deck, the hoist, and the material laydown area every day.

test.question: Under 1926.32(f), a "competent person" is one who:
options: Has worked at least 10 years in the trade
Can identify existing and predictable hazards and has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them
test.explanation: A competent person can identify existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions and has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them (1926.32(f)). Job-site scenario: a foreman who can spot a failing trench box but cannot stop work is not a competent person.

test.question: A scissor lift fails its pre-use check with a broken platform gate. Under 1926.20(b)(3), the employer must:
options: Tag it as unsafe or lock its controls so it cannot be operated, or physically remove it from the work area
Let the crew use it carefully until the end of the shift
Report it at the next weekly meeting
test.explanation: Machinery, tools, materials, or equipment that do not comply with Part 1926 are prohibited. They must be identified as unsafe by tagging or locking the controls to make them inoperable, or physically removed (1926.20(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: tag the lift "Do Not Operate" and lock out its controls until the gate is repaired.

test.question: Under 1926.20(b)(4), who may operate equipment and machinery on the job?
options: Only employees qualified by training or experience
Anyone with a valid driver's license
test.explanation: The employer may permit only employees qualified by training or experience to operate equipment and machinery (1926.20(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: a laborer with no skid-steer training cannot be told to "just move the pallets" with it.

test.question: What does 1926.21(b)(2) require every employer to do for each employee?
options: Give each employee a printed copy of Part 1926
Hold one company-wide orientation per year
Instruct each employee in recognizing and avoiding unsafe conditions and in the regulations that apply to their work environment
test.explanation: The employer must instruct each employee in the recognition and avoidance of unsafe conditions and the regulations applicable to their work environment (1926.21(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a new drywall hanger is shown the site's floor-opening, scaffold, and electrical hazards before starting work.

test.question: On a land-clearing job with poison ivy and venomous snakes, what does 1926.21(b)(4) require for exposed employees?
options: Nothing; plants and animals are not OSHA hazards
Only a first aid kit on site
Instruction on the potential hazards, how to avoid injury, and the first aid procedures to use if injured
test.explanation: Where harmful plants or animals are present, exposed employees must be instructed on the potential hazards, how to avoid injury, and the first aid procedures to use if injured (1926.21(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: the brush-clearing crew is briefed on identifying poison ivy, snake avoidance, and what to do after a bite.

test.question: Under 1926.25(a), form and scrap lumber with protruding nails must be:
options: Kept cleared from work areas, passageways, and stairs
Stacked at the end of each week
Left in place until framing is complete
test.explanation: Form and scrap lumber with protruding nails, and all other debris, must be kept cleared from work areas, passageways, and stairs in and around buildings (1926.25(a)). Job-site scenario: stripped forms are de-nailed or removed from the stairwell before the next crew comes through.

test.question: Under 1926.25(c), containers used for oily rags, flammable waste, or other hazardous wastes must be:
test.explanation: Containers for garbage and other oily, flammable, or hazardous wastes (caustics, acids, harmful dusts, etc.) must be equipped with covers (1926.25(c)). Job-site scenario: the painters' oily rags go into a lidded metal can, not an open bucket.

test.question: A remote pipeline job has no reasonably accessible clinic, hospital, or physician. What does 1926.50(c) require?
options: An ambulance on standby at all times
A person with a valid first-aid certificate (or verifiable equivalent training) available at the worksite to render first aid
test.explanation: Without a reasonably accessible infirmary, clinic, hospital, or physician, a person with a valid first-aid certificate (or equivalent training verifiable by documentation) must be available at the worksite (1926.50(c)). Job-site scenario: the foreman holds a current first-aid/CPR card and is on site whenever the crew works.

test.question: How often must the employer check the contents of a job-site first aid kit under 1926.50(d)(2)?
options: Only when the kit is opened
Before it is sent out on each job and at least weekly on each job
test.explanation: First aid kit contents must be in a weatherproof container and checked by the employer before being sent out on each job and at least weekly on each job, so used items get replaced (1926.50(d)(2)). Job-site scenario: the Monday toolbox talk includes restocking the gang-box first aid kit.

title: Personal Protective Equipment
topics: Noise exposure limits and hearing protection

test.question: Under 1926.95(c), the employer must ensure that all PPE:
options: Is selected to properly fit each affected employee
test.explanation: All PPE must be of safe design and construction for the work and be selected to properly fit each affected employee (1926.95(c)(1); 1926.95(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: a smaller worker gets a harness and gloves in their size, not the crew's spare XL.

test.question: A laborer is cutting concrete block with a saw that throws chips. Under 1926.102(a)(2), their eye protection must:
options: Provide side protection (clip-on or slide-on side shields are acceptable)
Be a face shield worn without glasses
test.explanation: When there is a hazard from flying objects, the employer must ensure eye protection with side protection is used. Detachable side protectors are acceptable (1926.102(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: safety glasses with side shields while cutting block. A face shield may be added, but 1926.102 does not specifically require it for this task.

test.question: When does 1926.100(a) require employees to wear protective helmets?
options: Where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, falling or flying objects, or electrical shock and burns
Only while a crane is operating
test.explanation: Employees working where there is a possible danger of head injury from impact, falling or flying objects, or electrical shock and burns must wear protective helmets (1926.100(a)). Workers exposed to high-voltage shock need helmets that meet the electrical insulation specifications (1926.100(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: everyone below an active steel deck wears a hard hat.

test.question: A worker will handle concrete admixtures that can burn skin. What governs the choice of gloves?
options: Leather gloves are acceptable for every task
PPE must be provided and used wherever chemical or other hazards could injure the body through absorption or contact, and be of safe design for the work
test.explanation: Protective equipment must be provided and used wherever chemical hazards (among others) can cause injury through absorption or physical contact (1926.95(a)), and must be of safe design for the work performed (1926.95(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: chemical-resistant gloves rated for the admixture, chosen from its SDS, rather than cotton or leather.

test.question: Under Table D-2 in 1926.52, what is the permissible daily exposure duration at 95 dBA (slow response)?
test.explanation: Table D-2 allows 4 hours per day at 95 dBA (8 hours at 90 dBA). Above table values, feasible engineering or administrative controls are required first, then PPE (1926.52(b)), and a continuing hearing conservation program (1926.52(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a jackhammer operator at 95 dBA without controls cannot exceed 4 hours.

test.question: Which item may an employer choose not to pay for under 1926.95(d)(2)?
options: Non-specialty safety-toe boots that the employer allows to be worn off the job site
Replacement for a respirator that wore out in normal use
test.explanation: Employers are not required to pay for non-specialty safety-toe footwear or non-specialty prescription safety eyewear if those items may be worn off the job site (1926.95(d)(2)). Other required PPE is provided at no cost (1926.95(d)(1)), including replacements except when lost or intentionally damaged (1926.95(d)(5)). Job-site scenario: standard steel-toe boots may be at the worker's expense, but the harness may not.

test.question: An employee brings their own safety glasses to work. Under 1926.95(b), the employer is responsible for:
options: Nothing; employee-owned PPE is the employee's responsibility
Assuring its adequacy, including proper maintenance and sanitation
test.explanation: Where employees provide their own protective equipment, the employer must assure its adequacy, including proper maintenance and sanitation (1926.95(b)). Job-site scenario: the foreman confirms the personal glasses are Z87-marked and not scratched before allowing them.

test.question: A carpenter wears prescription glasses while nailing. Under 1926.102(a)(3), they must wear:
options: Eye protection that incorporates the prescription, or that fits over the prescription lenses without disturbing either lens
test.explanation: Employees with prescription lenses who face eye hazards must wear eye protection that incorporates the prescription or that can be worn over the prescription lenses without disturbing the position of either (1926.102(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: over-the-glasses (OTG) safety goggles or prescription safety glasses.

test.question: Per Table E-1 in 1926.102(c)(1), what filter shade is listed as a guide for shielded metal-arc welding with 1/8-inch electrodes?
test.explanation: Table E-1 lists shade 10 for shielded metal-arc welding with 1/16- to 5/32-inch electrodes. Denser shades may be used to suit the individual (1926.102(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: a welder running 1/8-inch 7018 rod uses at least a shade 10 lens.

test.question: Which statement is consistent with 1926.101?
options: Plain cotton in the ears is acceptable hearing protection
Ear protective devices inserted in the ear must be fitted or determined individually by competent persons
Hearing protection is required only above 115 dBA
Earplugs may be shared between workers
test.explanation: Insert-type ear protective devices must be fitted or determined individually by competent persons (1926.101(b)), and plain cotton is not acceptable (1926.101(c)). Job-site scenario: new hires are shown how to roll and seat foam plugs, and their fit is checked.

title: Construction Site Communication
topics: Crane signal persons and signaling rules
Danger signs, caution signs, and accident prevention tags

resources.title: Safety Signs and Signals
resources.description: Accident prevention signs and tags standard

resources.title: Signaling (Flaggers)
resources.description: Flagger signaling must conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD

test.question: During a steel beam lift with several workers nearby, who may give signals to the crane operator?
options: Anyone who can see the load
Only one person at a time, although anyone who sees a safety problem may give a stop or emergency stop signal
Whoever the operator chooses for each pick
test.explanation: Only one person may give signals to a crane/derrick at a time (1926.1419(h)). Anyone who becomes aware of a safety problem must alert the operator or signal person with a stop or emergency stop signal (1926.1419(j)). Job-site scenario: the designated signal person directs the pick, but a connector who sees a snag can call "all stop."

test.question: Under 1926.201(a), signaling by flaggers, including the warning garments flaggers wear, must conform to:
options: Part 6 of the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD)
test.explanation: Flagger signaling, use of flaggers, and flaggers' warning garments must conform to Part 6 of the MUTCD (1926.201(a)). Traffic control devices must also conform to MUTCD Part 6 (1926.200(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: for night paving, the MUTCD Part 6 rules on flagger apparel and illumination apply.

test.question: Before opening an excavation, what does 1926.651(b)(1) require?
options: Determine the estimated location of underground utility installations that may reasonably be expected to be encountered
Start digging and watch for lines
test.explanation: The estimated location of utilities (sewer, telephone, fuel, electric, water, etc.) must be determined before opening an excavation (1926.651(b)(1)). Utility companies or owners must be contacted and asked to establish locations before digging starts (1926.651(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: call in the locate request and wait for marks before the excavator breaks ground.

test.question: Per Table U-1 in 1926.909, what is the warning signal before a blast?
options: A 1-minute series of long blasts 5 minutes before the blast signal
A single long blast 1 minute before
test.explanation: Table U-1: Warning signal is a 1-minute series of long blasts 5 minutes prior to the blast signal. Blast signal is a series of short blasts 1 minute prior to the shot. All clear is a prolonged blast after the blast area is inspected. The code must be posted, and employees must conform to it (1926.909(a)). Job-site scenario: the blaster sounds the long-blast series, waits 5 minutes, then gives the short-blast series.

test.question: How must exits be marked in a building under construction under 1926.34(b)?
options: Posted evacuation maps on every floor
By a readily visible sign; access to exits must also be marked where the exit is not immediately visible
No marking is required during construction
test.explanation: Exits must be marked by a readily visible sign, and access to exits must be marked where the exit or the way to reach it is not immediately visible (1926.34(b)). Job-site scenario: on an interior build-out with temporary partitions, add directional exit signs pointing to the stair.

test.question: Under 1926.200(b)(1), danger signs may be used only where:
options: Work has finished for the day
test.explanation: Danger signs are used only where an immediate hazard exists (1926.200(b)(1)) and have red as the predominating color for the upper panel (1926.200(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: "DANGER - Energized Equipment" at an open, live switchgear room.

test.question: Under 1926.200(c), caution signs have which predominating color, and what are they used for?
options: Yellow, to warn against potential hazards or caution against unsafe practices
test.explanation: Caution signs warn against potential hazards or caution against unsafe practices (1926.200(c)(1)) and have yellow as the predominating color (1926.200(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: "CAUTION - Watch Your Step" at a ramp transition.

test.question: Under 1926.200(h)(1), accident prevention tags are:
options: A permanent replacement for danger signs
A temporary means of warning of an existing hazard, such as defective tools or equipment
test.explanation: Accident prevention tags are a temporary means of warning employees of an existing hazard, such as defective tools or equipment. They may not substitute for accident prevention signs (1926.200(h)(1)). Job-site scenario: a "DO NOT USE" tag on a grinder with a cracked guard.

test.question: When crane signals are transmitted by radio, 1926.1420(c) requires that the operator receive them:
options: Through a handheld radio held to the ear
test.explanation: The operator's reception of signals must be hands-free (1926.1420(c)). The device must be tested on site before operations begin (1926.1420(a)). Job-site scenario: the operator wears a headset tied to a dedicated channel during a blind pick.

test.question: During a lift, radio contact between the operator and signal person drops out. Under 1926.1419(f), the operator must:
options: Accept hand signals from anyone nearby
Safely stop operations requiring signals until communication is re-established and a proper signal is given and understood
test.explanation: If the ability to transmit signals is interrupted, the operator must safely stop operations requiring signals until it is re-established and a proper signal is given and understood (1926.1419(f)). Job-site scenario: the radio battery dies mid-pick, so the operator holds the load until communication is restored.

title: Site Planning and Setup
topics: Material storage and floor load limits

resources.title: Employee Emergency Action Plans
resources.description: Required elements of construction emergency action plans

test.question: Steel will be staged on an elevated slab. What does 1926.250(a)(2) require?
options: Stored weight must not exceed maximum safe load limits, and floor load limits must be conspicuously posted in pounds per square foot (with listed exceptions)
Storage only on the ground floor
An engineer's stamp on every bundle
Nothing if the slab is concrete
test.explanation: Stored materials must not exceed maximum safe floor load limits (1926.250(a)(2)(i)), and those limits must be conspicuously posted in pounds per square foot in storage areas. Posting is not required for slab-on-grade or single-family and wood-framed multi-family residential structures (1926.250(a)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: confirm the slab rating with the engineer of record, post it, and stage the bundles accordingly.

test.question: Before haul trucks use a temporary haul road and ramp, 1926.602(a)(3)(i) requires that the access roadway or grade be:
options: Constructed and maintained to safely accommodate the movement of the equipment and vehicles involved
test.explanation: No employer may move construction equipment or vehicles on an access roadway or grade unless it is constructed and maintained to safely accommodate that equipment (1926.602(a)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: build up and grade the ramp out of the mass excavation before loaded trucks use it.

test.question: Before a mobile crane is set up, 1926.1402(b) requires that ground conditions be:
options: Firm, drained, and graded enough (with supporting materials if needed) to meet the manufacturer's support and level specifications
test.explanation: Equipment may not be assembled or used unless the ground is firm, drained (except marshes/wetlands), and graded enough, with supporting materials if needed, to meet the manufacturer's specifications for support and level (1926.1402(b)). Job-site scenario: crane mats over backfilled soil next to a new foundation wall.

test.question: Temporary power is being planned with 120-volt, 15/20-amp receptacles. What does 1926.404(b)(1) require to protect employees?
options: Extension cords from the nearest building
Ground-fault circuit interrupters, or an assured equipment grounding conductor program
test.explanation: The employer must use either GFCIs or an assured equipment grounding conductor program (1926.404(b)(1)(i)). 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles that are not part of the permanent wiring must have GFCIs if that option is used (1926.404(b)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: every temporary power spider box outlet is GFCI-protected.

test.question: When must provisions be made for prompt medical attention in case of serious injury, per 1926.50(b)?
options: Prior to commencement of the project
Only when more than 50 workers are on site
test.explanation: Provisions for prompt medical attention in case of serious injury must be made before the project starts (1926.50(b)). Emergency action plans required by a standard must include escape procedures, accounting for employees, and reporting means (1926.35(b)). Job-site scenario: identify the nearest trauma center and ambulance access route during mobilization.

test.question: A site crew has 15 employees, a sanitary sewer is not available, and the crew is not mobile. What is the minimum number of toilet facilities under Table D-1 in 1926.51(c)(1)?
options: None, if workers can drive somewhere
test.explanation: Table D-1 requires 1 toilet for 20 or fewer employees (1926.51(c)(1)). Job sites without a sanitary sewer use privies, chemical, recirculating, or combustion toilets (1926.51(c)(3)). The mobile-crew exception (1926.51(c)(4)) does not apply here. Job-site scenario: one chemical toilet for the 15-person crew.

test.question: Which statement about drinking water matches 1926.51(a)?
options: A common drinking cup is fine if rinsed
Any container with water in it is acceptable
Portable drinking-water containers must be able to be tightly closed and have a tap, and water may not be dipped from them
Employees must bring their own water
test.explanation: Portable containers used to dispense drinking water must be capable of being tightly closed and equipped with a tap, and water may not be dipped from them (1926.51(a)(2)). The common drinking cup is prohibited (1926.51(a)(4)). Job-site scenario: a lidded cooler with a spigot and single-use cups with a trash receptacle.

test.question: The site uses a cell phone system that does not automatically give 911 the caller's latitude and longitude. Under 1926.50(f)(2)(ii)(A), the employer must:
options: Post the company's home office address
Post the latitude and longitude of the worksite, or other location information that effectively communicates its location, in a conspicuous place
test.explanation: Where the communication system does not automatically supply latitude/longitude to 911, the employer must conspicuously post the worksite's latitude and longitude or other effective location-identification information (1926.50(f)(2)(ii)(A)). Job-site scenario: GPS coordinates and the gate address are posted at the trailer phone and the site entrance.

test.question: Per Table D-3 in 1926.56(a), what is the minimum illumination for concrete placement, excavation, and waste areas?
test.explanation: Table D-3 lists 3 foot-candles for general construction areas, concrete placement, excavation and waste areas, accessways, active storage areas, loading platforms, refueling, and field maintenance areas (1926.56(a)). Job-site scenario: light towers for a pre-dawn slab pour must deliver at least 3 foot-candles.

test.question: An employer with 8 employees has an emergency action plan required by an OSHA standard. Under 1926.35(e)(3), the plan:
options: May be communicated orally, and a written plan need not be kept
Needs to be reviewed only once a year
test.explanation: For employers with 10 or fewer employees, the plan may be communicated orally and a written plan need not be kept (1926.35(e)(3)). Job-site scenario: a small roofing crew's foreman verbally covers the escape route, meeting point, and how to report a fire.

title: Fire Prevention and Protection
topics: Portable fire extinguisher ratings, placement, and travel distance
Fire alarms, egress, and combustible debris

resources.title: Hot Work Fire Prevention
resources.description: Fire prevention for welding, cutting, and heating

test.question: More than 5 gallons of flammable liquid is being used on a jobsite. Under 1926.150(c)(1)(vi), what extinguisher must be provided within 50 feet?
test.explanation: A fire extinguisher rated at least 10B must be within 50 feet wherever more than 5 gallons of flammable or combustible liquids or 5 pounds of flammable gas are used. This does not apply to the integral fuel tanks of motor vehicles (1926.150(c)(1)(vi)). Job-site scenario: a 10B-rated (or higher) extinguisher at the fuel-can station for the gas-powered saws.

test.question: How must portable fire extinguishers be inspected and maintained under 1926.150?
options: Periodically, in accordance with NFPA No. 10A-1970, with defective equipment replaced immediately
test.explanation: Portable extinguishers must be inspected periodically and maintained in accordance with NFPA 10A-1970 (1926.150(c)(1)(viii)). All firefighting equipment must be kept in operating condition, and defective equipment replaced immediately (1926.150(a)(4)). The monthly interval in the original question is a 1910.157(e)(2) general-industry rule, not 1926 text. Job-site scenario: the safety lead checks extinguisher gauges and tags on a set schedule and swaps any discharged unit right away.

test.question: What is the maximum travel distance from any point of the protected area to the nearest fire extinguisher under 1926.150(c)(1)(i)?
test.explanation: One extinguisher rated at least 2A is required for each 3,000 square feet, and travel distance to the nearest extinguisher may not exceed 100 feet (1926.150(c)(1)(i)). Multistory buildings need at least one extinguisher on each floor, next to a stairway (1926.150(c)(1)(iv)). Job-site scenario: on a 200-foot-long floor plate, extinguishers at each stair core plus mid-floor.

test.question: A welding job is one where normal fire prevention precautions are not sufficient. Under 1926.352(e), how long must the extra fire-watch personnel guard against fire?
options: Only while welding is in progress
During the welding and for a sufficient period after completion to ensure no possibility of fire exists
Exactly 30 minutes after the work ends
Only if a hot work permit was issued
test.explanation: When normal precautions are not sufficient, additional personnel must guard against fire during the welding, cutting, or heating and for a sufficient period after completion to ensure no possibility of fire exists. They must be instructed on the anticipated hazards and firefighting equipment (1926.352(e)). 1926 sets no fixed number of minutes. The 30-minute figure is from the general-industry standard 1910.252(a)(2)(iii)(B). Job-site scenario: after welding clips near wood blocking, the fire watch stays until the area is cool and verified safe.

test.question: A beam that must be welded cannot be moved, and nearby wood blocking cannot be removed. What does 1926.352(b) require?
options: A written permit from the owner
Positive means to confine heat, sparks, and slag and to protect the immovable fire hazards from them
test.explanation: If the object cannot be moved and the fire hazards cannot all be removed, positive means must be taken to confine heat, sparks, and slag and to protect the immovable fire hazards (1926.352(b)). Movable fire hazards must first be taken to a safe place (1926.352(a)). Job-site scenario: welding blankets over the blocking and a spark-containment curtain around the work.

test.question: Under 1926.152(b)(1), what is the most flammable liquid that may be stored in a room outside an approved storage cabinet?
test.explanation: No more than 25 gallons of flammable liquids may be stored in a room outside an approved storage cabinet (1926.152(b)(1)). Quantities over 25 gallons go in an acceptable or approved cabinet (1926.152(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: once the paint thinner exceeds 25 gallons, the excess goes into the flammable cabinet.

test.question: Which is required for temporary heaters under 1926.154?
options: Heaters near tarps or canvas must be at least 10 feet from the coverings, and heaters in use must be set horizontally level unless the manufacturer's markings permit otherwise
A water source next to the heater
test.explanation: Heaters used near combustible tarpaulins, canvas, or similar coverings must be at least 10 feet from them (1926.154(b)(4)). Heaters in use must be set horizontally level unless manufacturer markings permit otherwise (1926.154(c)). Clearance to other combustibles follows Table F-4 (1926.154(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: a propane heater inside a tarped enclosure is set level and kept 10 feet from the tarps.

test.question: What does 1926.150(e) require for fire alarms on a construction site?
options: An alarm system (e.g., telephone system or siren) to alert employees and the local fire department, with the alarm code and reporting instructions posted at phones and employee entrances
No alarm until the building is occupied
A sprinkler system in every building
test.explanation: An alarm system must be established so employees on site and the local fire department can be alerted (1926.150(e)(1)). The alarm code and reporting instructions must be conspicuously posted at phones and employee entrances (1926.150(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: an air horn plus a posted "dial 911, give gate address" placard at each entrance.

test.question: What does 1926.34 require for exits in an occupied building under construction?
options: Two exit paths on every floor at all times
Free and unobstructed egress from all parts of the building while it is occupied, kept clear of obstructions
Exits only on the ground floor
test.explanation: Exits must provide free and unobstructed egress from all parts of the building at all times when it is occupied (1926.34(a)), and means of egress must be kept free of obstructions (1926.34(c)). Job-site scenario: drywall pallets are not staged in the stair corridor.

test.question: How must combustible scrap and debris be handled under 1926.25(b)?
options: Removed only at the end of the project
Removed at regular intervals during construction, with safe means provided for removal
test.explanation: Combustible scrap and debris must be removed at regular intervals during construction, and safe means must be provided for removal (1926.25(b)). Daily removal is good practice but is not the regulatory wording. Job-site scenario: framers fill the dumpster by chute at the end of each shift.

title: Material Handling and Storage
topics: Stacking limits for lumber, brick, and block
Storage on scaffolds and near openings
Posted floor loads and forklift capacity

resources.title: Disposal of Waste Materials
resources.description: Chutes, debris drop areas, and waste removal

test.question: Under 1926.250(b)(8)(iv), lumber that will be handled manually may be stacked no higher than:
test.explanation: Lumber piles may not exceed 20 feet, and lumber to be handled manually may not be stacked more than 16 feet high (1926.250(b)(8)(iv)). Job-site scenario: a hand-loaded stack of 2x10s tops out at 16 feet.

test.question: When must rigging equipment for material handling be inspected under 1926.251(a)(1)?
options: Prior to use on each shift, and as necessary during use
test.explanation: Rigging equipment must be inspected before use on each shift and as necessary during use, and defective rigging removed from service (1926.251(a)(1)). Slings and fastenings must be inspected each day before use by a competent person (1926.251(a)(6)). Job-site scenario: the rigger checks wire rope slings for broken wires and kinks before the first steel pick of the shift.

test.question: How must materials that are not compatible with each other be stored under 1926.250(b)(3)?
test.explanation: Noncompatible materials must be segregated in storage (1926.250(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: oxidizers and fuels are not stored in the same conex. Indoors, noncompatible materials that create a fire hazard need a 1-hour fire-resistant barrier (1926.151(d)(3)).

test.question: Under 1926.250(b)(5), how much material may be stored on a scaffold or runway?
options: Up to the rated capacity overnight
No more than the supplies needed for immediate operations
test.explanation: Materials may not be stored on scaffolds or runways beyond the supplies needed for immediate operations (1926.250(b)(5)). Job-site scenario: masons stage only the brick and mortar for the current lift.

test.question: How must compressed gas cylinders be kept under 1926.350(a)?
options: Secured upright, with oxygen in storage separated from fuel-gas cylinders by at least 20 feet or by a 5-foot-high noncombustible barrier with at least a half-hour fire rating
Oxygen and acetylene chained together side by side in storage
test.explanation: Cylinders must be secured upright at all times except briefly while hoisted or carried (1926.350(a)(9)). Oxygen in storage must be separated from fuel gas or combustibles by at least 20 feet or by a noncombustible barrier at least 5 feet high with at least a half-hour fire-resistance rating (1926.350(a)(10)). Job-site scenario: oxygen and acetylene cages placed 20+ feet apart.

test.question: Inside a building under construction, material may not be stored within ___ of any hoistway or inside floor opening (1926.250(b)(1)).
test.explanation: Material may not be placed within 6 feet of any hoistway or inside floor opening, or within 10 feet of an exterior wall that does not extend above the top of the stored material (1926.250(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: drywall carts are kept back from the open elevator shaft.

test.question: What is the maximum height of a brick stack under 1926.250(b)(6)?
test.explanation: Brick stacks may not exceed 7 feet. When a loose brick stack reaches 4 feet, it must be tapered back 2 inches for every foot above the 4-foot level (1926.250(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: a loose stack at 5 feet is stepped back 2 inches from the 4-foot mark.

test.question: What must be conspicuously posted in storage areas on elevated floors under 1926.250(a)(2)(ii)?
options: Maximum safe floor load limits in pounds per square foot
test.explanation: Employers must conspicuously post maximum safe floor load limits, in pounds per square foot, in all storage areas, except slab-on-grade and certain residential structures (1926.250(a)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: "Max 50 psf" signs on the second-floor deck.

test.question: Under 1926.250(b)(7), masonry blocks stacked higher than 6 feet must be:
options: Tapered back one-half block per tier above the 6-foot level
test.explanation: When masonry blocks are stacked higher than 6 feet, the stack must be tapered back one-half block per tier above the 6-foot level (1926.250(b)(7)). Job-site scenario: an 8-foot CMU stack steps back half a block on each tier above 6 feet.

test.question: Under 1926.602(c)(1)(i), what must be displayed on a forklift (lift truck)?
options: Its rated capacity, clearly posted where the operator can see it, and not exceeded
test.explanation: Lift trucks must have their rated capacity clearly posted on the vehicle where the operator can see it, including alternate ratings for removable counterweights. These ratings may not be exceeded (1926.602(c)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the operator checks the data plate before lifting a pallet of block.

resources.title: Power-Operated Hand Tools
resources.description: Electric, pneumatic, fuel, hydraulic, and powder-actuated tools

test.question: Under 1926.300(a), hand and power tools must be kept in a safe condition:
options: Only if the employer owns them
Whether furnished by the employer or the employee
test.explanation: All hand and power tools and similar equipment, whether furnished by the employer or the employee, must be maintained in a safe condition (1926.300(a)). Job-site scenario: a worker's personal circular saw with a frayed cord is held to the same rule as company tools.

test.question: What does 1926.302(b)(1) require for pneumatic tool connections?
options: Securing the tool to the hose or whip by some positive means to prevent accidental disconnection
test.explanation: Pneumatic power tools must be secured to the hose or whip by some positive means to prevent accidental disconnection (1926.302(b)(1)). Hoses over 1/2-inch inside diameter need a safety device at the supply source or branch line to reduce pressure if the hose fails (1926.302(b)(7)). Job-site scenario: a retaining clip on the nailer fitting and an excess-flow valve on the 3/4-inch compressor line.

test.question: A hammer with a cracked wooden handle is found on site. What is required?
options: Remove it from use; employers may not issue or permit unsafe hand tools, and wooden handles must be free of splinters or cracks
test.explanation: Employers may not issue or permit the use of unsafe hand tools (1926.301(a)), and wooden handles must be kept free of splinters or cracks and tight in the tool (1926.301(d)). Noncompliant tools must be tagged or physically removed (1926.20(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: tag the hammer "Do Not Use" and take it out of the gang box.

test.question: Who may operate a powder-actuated tool under 1926.302(e)(1)?
options: Only employees trained in the operation of the particular tool in use
Anyone with five years of experience
test.explanation: Only employees trained in the operation of the particular tool in use may operate a powder-actuated tool (1926.302(e)(1)). The tool must be tested each day before loading (1926.302(e)(2)). Manufacturer operator cards are common practice, but the regulation says "trained." Job-site scenario: the electrician trained on the Hilti DX model uses that tool, not an unfamiliar brand.

test.question: When must power-operated tools that are designed to accommodate guards have them?
options: Whenever the tool is in use
test.explanation: Power-operated tools designed to accommodate guards must be equipped with those guards when in use (1926.300(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the angle grinder's guard stays on while cutting rebar.

test.question: What PPE must be provided to employees using hand and power tools under 1926.300(c)?
options: The particular PPE needed to protect against falling, flying, abrasive, and splashing objects, or harmful dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, or gases
test.explanation: Employees exposed to falling, flying, abrasive, or splashing objects, or to harmful dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, or gases, must be given the particular PPE needed to protect them from the hazard (1926.300(c)). Job-site scenario: a concrete saw operator gets eye and face protection, hearing protection, and respiratory protection as the exposure requires.

test.question: May a worker lower a drill from a scaffold by its electric cord?
options: No; electric cords may not be used for hoisting or lowering tools
Yes, if the cord is heavy duty
Yes, if the drop is less than 10 feet
test.explanation: Electric cords may not be used for hoisting or lowering tools (1926.302(a)(2)). The same applies to pneumatic hoses (1926.302(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: use a hand line and tool bucket instead.

test.question: Under 1926.302(a)(1), electric power-operated tools must be:
options: Either of the approved double-insulated type or grounded in accordance with Subpart K
test.explanation: Electric power-operated tools must be either of the approved double-insulated type or grounded in accordance with Subpart K (1926.302(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a corded drill with a broken ground pin is taken out of service unless it is double-insulated.

test.question: What guarding does 1926.304(d) require on portable power-driven circular saws?
options: The lower guard may be pinned back for deep cuts
Guards above and below the base plate or shoe, with the lower guard automatically returning to the covering position
No guard is required on cordless saws
test.explanation: Portable circular saws must have guards above and below the base plate or shoe, and the lower guard must automatically and instantly return to the covering position when the tool is withdrawn (1926.304(d)). Job-site scenario: never wedge the lower guard open to rip plywood.

test.question: Under 1926.301(c), impact tools such as drift pins, wedges, and chisels must be:
test.explanation: Impact tools such as drift pins, wedges, and chisels must be kept free of mushroomed heads (1926.301(c)). Job-site scenario: a cold chisel with a flared striking face is dressed or replaced before use.

title: Heavy Equipment Operation
topics: When a signal person is needed

resources.title: Motor Vehicles
resources.description: Brakes, alarms, and shift inspection of motor vehicles

test.question: Under 1926.601(b)(14), when must job-site motor vehicles be checked to make sure brakes, tires, horn, steering, seat belts, and safety devices are in safe operating condition?
options: At the beginning of each shift, with defects corrected before the vehicle is placed in service
Only when the operator notices a problem
test.explanation: All vehicles in use must be checked at the beginning of each shift, and all defects corrected before the vehicle is placed in service (1926.601(b)(14)). Job-site scenario: the dump truck driver walks around and checks brakes, horn, and lights before the first load.

test.question: A loader with an obstructed rear view must back up. Under 1926.602(a)(9)(ii), what is required?
options: A reverse signal alarm distinguishable from the surrounding noise, or an employee who signals that it is safe
test.explanation: Earthmoving or compacting equipment with an obstructed rear view may not be used in reverse unless it has a working reverse signal alarm distinguishable from the surrounding noise, or an employee signals that it is safe (1926.602(a)(9)(ii)). Job-site scenario: in a congested yard, a spotter guides the loader in addition to the backup alarm.

test.question: A dozer blade will be serviced. What does 1926.600(a)(3)(i) require?
options: Raise the blade for better access
Leave the engine running for hydraulics
Blades, buckets, and dump bodies must be fully lowered or blocked when being repaired or when not in use
test.explanation: Bulldozer and scraper blades, end-loader buckets, dump bodies, and similar equipment must be fully lowered or blocked when being repaired or not in use, with controls in neutral, motors stopped, and brakes set (1926.600(a)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: the mechanic cribs the raised blade before reaching under it.

test.question: Before an employee operates a crane covered by Subpart CC, what must the employer ensure under 1926.1427(a)?
options: That the operator has a valid driver's license
That the operator has two years of experience
That the operator is trained, certified/licensed, and evaluated in accordance with 1926.1427 (except for listed equipment)
test.explanation: The employer must ensure each operator is trained, certified/licensed, and evaluated under 1926.1427 before operating Subpart CC equipment, except the equipment listed in 1926.1427(a)(2): derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment rated 2,000 lb or less (1926.1427(a)). Job-site scenario: the mobile crane operator holds an accredited certification for that crane type and has been evaluated by the employer.

test.question: What does 1926.152(g)(10) require when equipment is being refueled?
options: The motors of all equipment being fueled must be shut off during fueling
Refueling only at the end of the shift
test.explanation: The motors of all equipment being fueled must be shut off during the fueling operation (1926.152(g)(10)). There must be no smoking or open flames in fueling areas (1926.152(g)(8)). Letting hot parts cool is good practice but is not in this paragraph. Job-site scenario: the skid steer is shut down before the fuel nozzle goes in.

test.question: How must equipment be parked under 1926.600(a)(3)(ii)?
options: With the parking brake set, and on inclines with the wheels chocked and the parking brake set
test.explanation: Whenever equipment is parked, the parking brake must be set. Equipment parked on an incline must also have its wheels chocked (1926.600(a)(3)(ii)). Blades and buckets are lowered when not in use (1926.600(a)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: a backhoe parked on the ramp is chocked with the brake set and bucket grounded.

test.question: A contractor wants to add fork extensions to a lift truck. What does 1926.602(c)(1)(ii) require?
options: The manufacturer's written approval for modifications that affect capacity or safe operation, with the capacity and instruction plates changed accordingly
test.explanation: No modifications or additions that affect capacity or safe operation may be made without the manufacturer's written approval. Capacity, operation, and maintenance plates must be updated, and the original safety factor may not be reduced (1926.602(c)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: get the forklift maker's written approval and updated data plate before using extensions.

test.question: An excavator will work near a 7,200-volt overhead distribution line. What is the minimum clearance between the line and any part of the equipment or load under 1926.600(a)(6)(i)?
test.explanation: For lines rated 50 kV or below, the minimum clearance is 10 feet (1926.600(a)(6)(i)). Any overhead wire is considered energized until the owner says otherwise and it is visibly grounded (1926.600(a)(6)(vi)). Cranes and derricks follow Subpart CC (1926.1408) instead. Job-site scenario: mark a 10-foot limit and use a dedicated observer where clearance is hard to judge (1926.600(a)(6)(iv)).

test.question: Under 1926.602(a)(2), seat belts must be provided on earthmoving equipment except:
options: On equipment designed only for stand-up operation, or equipment without ROPS or adequate canopy protection
On any equipment used on site only
When the operator prefers not to wear one
test.explanation: Seat belts are required on equipment covered by 1926.602(a), but are not required on equipment designed only for stand-up operation or on equipment without ROPS or adequate canopy protection (1926.602(a)(2)(i)-(iii)). Job-site scenario: the dozer has ROPS, so the operator belts in.

test.question: Under 1926.1419(a)(1), a signal person must be provided when:
options: The point of operation (load travel or the area near or at load placement) is not in full view of the operator
Only when the operator requests one
test.explanation: A signal person is required when the point of operation is not in full view of the operator (1926.1419(a)(1)). Signal persons are also required when the view in the direction of travel is obstructed, or when the operator or the person handling the load decides one is needed (1926.1419(a)(2)-(3)). Job-site scenario: the crane places a concrete bucket behind a wall the operator cannot see.

resources.title: Scaffold Inspection Requirement
resources.description: Competent-person inspection before each work shift

test.question: What is the minimum width of a scaffold platform or walkway under 1926.451(b)(2), apart from the listed exceptions?
test.explanation: Each scaffold platform and walkway must be at least 18 inches wide, except as provided in 1926.451(b)(2)(i)-(ii) (1926.451(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a bricklaying platform on a mobile scaffold uses at least 18 inches of planking.

test.question: When is fall protection required for an employee on a scaffold under 1926.451(g)(1)?
options: Only while the scaffold is being moved
When the employee is more than 10 feet above a lower level
test.explanation: Each employee on a scaffold more than 10 feet above a lower level must be protected from falling to that lower level (1926.451(g)(1)). Job-site scenario: a 12-foot mobile tower for window installation needs guardrails (or a PFAS where (g)(1) calls for one).

test.question: A supported scaffold has a height-to-base width ratio (including outriggers) of more than 4:1. What does 1926.451(c)(1) require?
options: It must be restrained from tipping by guying, tying, bracing, or equivalent means
Nothing, if the casters are locked
It may not be used at all
A second ladder must be added
test.explanation: Supported scaffolds with a height-to-base width ratio over 4:1 (including outriggers) must be restrained from tipping by guying, tying, bracing, or equivalent means (1926.451(c)(1)). 4:1 is the point at which restraint is required, not an absolute maximum. Job-site scenario: a 20-foot tower on a 4-foot base (5:1) must be tied in or have outriggers added.

test.question: How often must scaffolds be inspected under 1926.451(f)(3)?
options: By a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity
test.explanation: Scaffolds and components must be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity (1926.451(f)(3)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks the tower before drywall work starts and again after a forklift bumps it.

test.question: What does 1926.452(w)(10) require before a mobile scaffold is moved?
options: Each employee on the scaffold must be made aware of the move
test.explanation: Before a scaffold is moved, each employee on it must be made aware of the move (1926.452(w)(10)). Employees may ride only if all conditions in 1926.452(w)(6) are met: surface within 3 degrees of level, height-to-base 2:1 or less during movement (unless designed otherwise), outriggers on both sides if used, powered speed no more than 1 ft/s, and no one beyond the wheels. Job-site scenario: the painter on the platform is told before the tower is rolled.

test.question: For employees to ride a mobile scaffold while it is moved, 1926.452(w)(6)(i) requires the surface to be:
options: Within 3 degrees of level and free of pits, holes, and obstructions
test.explanation: Employees may not ride unless the surface is within 3 degrees of level and free of pits, holes, and obstructions, along with the other (w)(6) conditions (1926.452(w)(6)(i)). Supported scaffolds must bear on base plates and mud sills or another adequate firm foundation (1926.451(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: no riding across the sloped, rutted gravel apron.

test.question: A mobile scaffold platform is 12 feet above the floor. How must workers reach it under 1926.451(e)(1)?
options: By a ladder, stair tower, ramp, or other listed means, because the platform is more than 2 feet above the point of access; crossbraces may not be used
By jumping up from a ladder
test.explanation: When platforms are more than 2 feet above or below a point of access, portable, hook-on, or attachable ladders, stair towers, ramps, walkways, integral prefabricated access, or direct access from another surface must be used. Crossbraces may not be used as a means of access (1926.451(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: use the tower's built-in ladder frame, not the X-braces.

test.question: At what wind speed does 1926.451(f)(12) prohibit work on scaffolds?
options: No set speed; work is prohibited during storms or high winds unless a competent person decides it is safe and employees are protected by a personal fall arrest system or wind screens
test.explanation: Work on or from scaffolds is prohibited during storms or high winds unless a competent person decides it is safe and employees are protected by a PFAS or wind screens. Wind screens may be used only if the scaffold is secured against the wind forces (1926.451(f)(12)). No numeric wind speed is set. Job-site scenario: the competent person stops facade work when gusts start rocking the tower.

test.question: Under 1926.452(w)(7), may a mobile scaffold platform extend outward beyond the base supports?
options: Yes, if the height is under 3 times the base
No, unless outrigger frames or equivalent devices are used to ensure stability
test.explanation: Platforms may not extend outward beyond the base supports of the scaffold unless outrigger frames or equivalent devices are used to ensure stability (1926.452(w)(7)). Job-site scenario: a cantilevered side bracket is not used on the tower without outriggers.

test.question: A mobile scaffold is being used in place, not moving. What does 1926.452(w)(2) require of its casters and wheels?
options: They must be chocked with scrap lumber
Workers should stand near the wheels
They must be locked with positive wheel and/or wheel-and-swivel locks, or equivalent means, to prevent movement
test.explanation: Casters and wheels must be locked with positive wheel and/or wheel-and-swivel locks, or equivalent, to prevent movement while the scaffold is used in a stationary manner (1926.452(w)(2)). Scaffolds must support their own weight plus at least 4 times the maximum intended load (1926.451(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: lock all four casters before climbing up to set ductwork.

title: Fall Protection Basics
topics: Free fall and inspection of personal fall arrest systems

resources.title: Personal Fall Arrest Systems
resources.description: Fall protection systems criteria and practices

test.question: At what height above a lower level does 1926.501(b)(1) require fall protection for an employee at an unprotected side or edge?
test.explanation: Employees on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems (1926.501(b)(1)). Residential construction uses the same 6-foot trigger (1926.501(b)(13)). Job-site scenario: framers setting roof trusses 8 feet up need one of those systems.

test.question: What minimum breaking strength does 1926.502(d)(9) require for lanyards and vertical lifelines?
test.explanation: Lanyards and vertical lifelines must have a minimum breaking strength of 5,000 pounds (1926.502(d)(9)). Horizontal lifelines are handled differently: they must be designed, installed, and used under the supervision of a qualified person (1926.502(d)(8)). Job-site scenario: the roofer's rope grab and vertical lifeline are rated 5,000 lb.

test.question: How often must personal fall arrest systems be inspected under 1926.502(d)(21)?
options: Prior to each use, with defective components removed from service
test.explanation: Personal fall arrest systems must be inspected before each use for wear, damage, and other deterioration, and defective components removed from service (1926.502(d)(21)). Job-site scenario: the ironworker checks harness webbing, stitching, D-ring, and lanyard snap hooks before tying off.

test.question: On a low-slope roof where no mechanical equipment is being used, how far from the roof edge must a warning line be erected under 1926.502(f)(1)(i)?
test.explanation: When mechanical equipment is not being used, the warning line must be at least 6 feet from the roof edge (1926.502(f)(1)(i)). With mechanical equipment, it must be at least 6 feet from edges parallel to the equipment's direction of travel and 10 feet from edges perpendicular to it (1926.502(f)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: HVAC crews hand-carrying parts work inside a line set 6 feet back.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(1), how far below the working surface may a safety net be installed?
options: As close as practicable, and never more than 30 feet below
test.explanation: Safety nets must be installed as close as practicable under the working surface, and never more than 30 feet below it (1926.502(c)(1)). Nets are one of three accepted systems, along with guardrails and personal fall arrest (1926.501(b)(1)). They are not limited to cases where other systems are infeasible. Job-site scenario: on a bridge deck, the net hangs directly below the work area with nothing obstructing the fall zone.

test.question: Under 1926.502(d)(16)(iii), a personal fall arrest system must be rigged so the employee can free fall no more than:
test.explanation: A personal fall arrest system must be rigged so the employee can neither free fall more than 6 feet nor contact any lower level (1926.502(d)(16)(iii)). Maximum arresting force with a body harness is 1,800 pounds (1926.502(d)(16)(ii)). Job-site scenario: an ironworker ties off overhead with a 6-foot lanyard so the free fall stays under 6 feet.

test.question: Under 1926.502(d)(15), anchorages for personal fall arrest equipment must be independent of platform supports and either support at least ___ per employee attached, or be designed by a qualified person with a safety factor of at least two.
test.explanation: Anchorages must be independent of any anchorage supporting platforms and capable of supporting at least 5,000 pounds per employee attached. Alternatively, they can be part of a complete system with a safety factor of at least two, under the supervision of a qualified person (1926.502(d)(15)). Job-site scenario: a roof anchor for two workers either holds 10,000 lb or is engineered by a qualified person.

test.question: What does 1926.502(i) require of covers over floor holes?
options: They are only temporary and need no marking
They must support at least twice the weight imposed on them, be secured against displacement, and be color coded or marked "HOLE" or "COVER"
test.explanation: Covers must support at least twice the weight of employees, equipment, and materials that may be imposed on them (1926.502(i)(2)), be secured against accidental displacement (1926.502(i)(3)), and be color coded or marked "HOLE" or "COVER" (1926.502(i)(4)). Job-site scenario: a plywood cover over a slab penetration is screwed down and spray-painted "HOLE."

test.question: Under 1926.502(b)(1), what is the required top-edge height of a guardrail system's top rail?
test.explanation: The top rail must be 42 inches plus or minus 3 inches above the walking/working level (1926.502(b)(1)). It must withstand at least 200 pounds applied within 2 inches of the top edge, outward or downward (1926.502(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: a perimeter cable is set between 39 and 45 inches above the deck.

test.question: Under 1926.503(a), who must train employees who might be exposed to fall hazards?
options: A competent person qualified in the listed areas
The employee may self-train using the manufacturer's manual
test.explanation: The employer must provide a training program for each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards (1926.503(a)(1)), with training given by a competent person qualified in the listed areas (1926.503(a)(2)). Training must be certified in writing (1926.503(b)(1)), and retraining is required when an employee lacks understanding or skill (1926.503(c)). Job-site scenario: new hires are trained by the site's competent person before going up on the deck.

title: Ladder Safety
topics: Competent-person inspections and removing defective ladders

resources.title: Ladder Use Requirements
resources.description: Rules for using all ladders, including job-made ladders

test.question: At what angle must a non-self-supporting ladder be set under 1926.1053(b)(5)(i)?
options: About 4:1 (horizontal distance at the foot is about one-quarter of the working length)
test.explanation: Non-self-supporting ladders must be set so the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot is approximately one-quarter of the working length, roughly a 4:1 ratio (1926.1053(b)(5)(i)). Job-site scenario: an extension ladder with 20 feet of working length has its foot about 5 feet out from the wall.

test.question: When a portable ladder is used to reach an upper landing, how far must its side rails extend above the landing under 1926.1053(b)(1)?
test.explanation: Side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the upper landing surface. If that is not possible, the ladder must be secured at its top to a rigid support and a grasping device provided (1926.1053(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the extension ladder to the roof sticks up 3 feet past the eave.

test.question: What inspection does 1926.1053(b)(15) require for ladders?
options: Inspection by a competent person for visible defects periodically and after any occurrence that could affect safe use
test.explanation: Ladders must be inspected by a competent person for visible defects on a periodic basis and after any occurrence that could affect their safe use (1926.1053(b)(15)). Checking before each use is good practice, but the standard sets the competent-person inspection. Job-site scenario: after a stepladder is knocked over by a forklift, the competent person inspects it before reuse.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(a)(1), a portable ladder must be able to support at least how much without failure?
options: Four times the maximum intended load (3.3 times for extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladders)
test.explanation: Self-supporting and non-self-supporting portable ladders must support at least four times the maximum intended load, except extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladders, which must sustain at least 3.3 times (1926.1053(a)(1)(i)-(ii)). Ladders may not be loaded beyond their maximum intended load or rated capacity (1926.1053(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: pick a ladder whose rating covers the worker plus tools and materials.

test.question: A ladder is found with a split side rail. What does 1926.1053(b)(16) require?
options: Keep using it until the end of the job
Mark it as defective or tag it "Do Not Use", and withdraw it from service until repaired
test.explanation: Portable ladders with structural defects such as broken or split rails must be immediately marked as defective or tagged "Do Not Use" (or similar) and withdrawn from service until repaired (1926.1053(b)(16)). Repairs must restore the original design criteria (1926.1053(b)(18)). Job-site scenario: the split ladder is tagged and removed from the job.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(b)(6), on what surfaces may ladders be used?
options: Any surface if someone holds the ladder
Only on stable and level surfaces, unless secured to prevent accidental displacement
test.explanation: Ladders may be used only on stable and level surfaces unless secured against accidental displacement (1926.1053(b)(6)). On slippery surfaces they must be secured or have slip-resistant feet (1926.1053(b)(7)). Job-site scenario: on soft soil, set the ladder on a firm, level base and secure it.

test.question: What does 1926.1053(b)(22) say about carrying items on a ladder?
options: An employee may not carry any object or load that could cause them to lose balance and fall
Anything may be carried in one hand
Tools may only be carried in pockets
test.explanation: An employee may not carry any object or load that could cause them to lose balance and fall (1926.1053(b)(22)). At least one hand must grasp the ladder while climbing (1926.1053(b)(21)), and the user must face the ladder (1926.1053(b)(20)). Job-site scenario: the electrician uses a tool belt and hoists the conduit bundle up by hand line.

test.question: A ladder is set up in a doorway where foot traffic could knock it. What does 1926.1053(b)(8) require?
options: Secure the ladder to prevent accidental displacement, or barricade to keep traffic away
Only tie it off above 20 feet
test.explanation: Ladders placed where workplace activities or traffic could displace them, such as passageways, doorways, or driveways, must be secured or barricaded (1926.1053(b)(8)). Job-site scenario: cones and caution tape route traffic around a ladder in a corridor door.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(b)(12), what kind of ladder is required where the employee or ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment?
options: An aluminum ladder with rubber feet
A wooden ladder painted with opaque coating
test.explanation: Ladders must have nonconductive siderails if used where the employee or ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment, except as provided in 1926.955 (1926.1053(b)(12)). Wood ladders may not be coated with an opaque covering (1926.1053(a)(12)). Job-site scenario: a fiberglass stepladder is used to work near an open panel.

test.question: What does 1926.1053(b)(13) say about the top of a stepladder?
options: It may be used if someone holds the ladder
Standing on it is fine for short tasks
The second step from the top is also prohibited
The top or top step may not be used as a step
test.explanation: The top or top step of a stepladder may not be used as a step (1926.1053(b)(13)). The "two steps down" rule is manufacturer and ANSI labeling, not 1926 text. Job-site scenario: if the painter needs the top step to reach, get a taller ladder.

test.question: Where platforms are overlapped to make a longer platform, what does 1926.451(b)(7) require?
options: The overlap must occur only over supports and be at least 12 inches, unless the platforms are nailed together or otherwise restrained
The overlap must be at least 6 inches anywhere
The overlap must be 18 inches between supports
No overlap is needed if cleated
test.explanation: Overlaps must occur only over supports and be at least 12 inches, unless the platforms are nailed together or otherwise restrained (1926.451(b)(7)). Separately, each platform end must extend over the centerline of its support by at least 6 inches unless cleated or restrained (1926.451(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: two planks overlap 12 inches directly over a frame bearer.

test.question: Who must inspect scaffolds before each work shift under 1926.451(f)(3)?
test.explanation: Scaffolds and components must be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity (1926.451(f)(3)). Job-site scenario: the designated competent person tags the scaffold green after the morning inspection.

test.question: Under 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled, or altered only:
options: After an engineer stamps the drawing
Under the supervision and direction of a competent person qualified in those activities, by experienced and trained employees selected for the work
test.explanation: Erecting, moving, dismantling, or altering scaffolds must be done only under the supervision and direction of a qualified competent person, by experienced and trained employees selected by that competent person (1926.451(f)(7)). Job-site scenario: the scaffold foreman directs a trained crew when adding a lift.

test.question: When there is a danger of tools or materials falling from a scaffold onto employees below, which does 1926.451(h)(2) require?
options: Toeboards on every scaffold at all heights
Only hard hats for workers below
Nothing if the scaffold is under 20 feet
Either barricade the area below and keep employees out, or erect a toeboard along platform edges more than 10 feet above lower levels
test.explanation: Where objects could fall and strike employees below, either barricade the area below and keep employees out (1926.451(h)(2)(i)), or install a toeboard along platform edges more than 10 feet above lower levels (1926.451(h)(2)(ii)). Toeboards must be at least 3.5 inches high and withstand 50 pounds (1926.451(h)(4)). Job-site scenario: masons 14 feet up get toeboards because the sidewalk below stays open.

test.question: Under 1926.451(b)(3), how far may the front edge of a platform be from the face of the work unless guardrails or personal fall arrest are used?
test.explanation: The front edge of platforms may not be more than 14 inches from the face of the work unless guardrails are erected along the front edge and/or personal fall arrest systems are used, with listed exceptions (1926.451(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: bricklayers keep the platform within 14 inches of the wall.

test.question: How often must suspension scaffold ropes be inspected under 1926.451(d)(10)?
options: By a competent person prior to each workshift and after every occurrence that could affect the rope's integrity
test.explanation: Ropes must be inspected for defects by a competent person before each workshift and after every occurrence that could affect their integrity, and replaced if listed conditions exist (1926.451(d)(10)). Job-site scenario: the window-washing crew's competent person checks the ropes for broken wires each morning.

test.question: Where must the bottom rung of a hook-on or attachable scaffold ladder be positioned under 1926.451(e)(2)(ii)?
options: No more than 36 inches above grade
No more than 24 inches above the scaffold supporting level
test.explanation: Hook-on and attachable ladders must be positioned so their bottom rung is no more than 24 inches above the scaffold supporting level (1926.451(e)(2)(ii)). Ladders or other listed access are required when platforms are more than 2 feet above or below the access point (1926.451(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: after grading, the attachable ladder is extended so the first rung is within 24 inches of the ground.

test.question: How must fabricated frame scaffolds be braced under 1926.452(c)(2)?
options: By cross, horizontal, or diagonal braces (or a combination) that secure vertical members together laterally, with all brace connections secured
test.explanation: Frames and panels must be braced by cross, horizontal, or diagonal braces, or a combination, that secure vertical members together laterally and keep the scaffold plumb, level, and square. All brace connections must be secured (1926.452(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: every frame set gets its cross braces pinned before planking.

test.question: What load must each suspension rope on a non-adjustable suspension scaffold support under 1926.451(a)(3)?
test.explanation: Each suspension rope and its connecting hardware must support at least 6 times the maximum intended load (1926.451(a)(3)). Adjustable suspension scaffolds also require 6 times, calculated at the greater of the hoist's rated load or twice its stall load (1926.451(a)(4)). Job-site scenario: rigging for a two-point swing stage is checked against the 6:1 requirement.

test.question: A scaffold frame member is bent. What does 1926.451(f)(4) require?
options: Immediately repair, replace, or brace it to meet capacity requirements, or remove it from service until repaired
Report it at the weekly meeting
test.explanation: Any scaffold part damaged or weakened below the required strength must be immediately repaired or replaced, braced to meet the capacity provisions, or removed from service until repaired (1926.451(f)(4)). Job-site scenario: the bent frame is swapped out before work resumes.

title: Steel Erection Safety
topics: Fall protection triggers for steel erection and connectors

resources.title: Steel Erection Fall Protection
resources.description: Fall protection for steel erection, connectors, and controlled decking zones

test.question: Under 1926.760(b)(1), connectors must be protected from fall hazards of more than:
options: Two stories or 30 feet above a lower level, whichever is less
test.explanation: Connectors must be protected from fall hazards of more than two stories or 30 feet above a lower level, whichever is less (1926.760(b)(1)). At heights over 15 and up to 30 feet, they must be provided with a personal fall arrest, positioning, or restraint system and wear the equipment needed to tie off (1926.760(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: on a building with 12-foot stories, a connector at 25 feet (above two stories) must be protected.

test.question: Before steel erection begins, what does 1926.752(b) require the steel erector to have received?
options: Written notification that the concrete in footings, piers, and walls (or masonry mortar) has reached 75% of design strength or enough strength to support erection loads
test.explanation: A steel erector may not erect steel without written notification that the concrete or mortar has reached, based on an appropriate ASTM test of field-cured samples, 75% of the intended minimum compressive design strength or enough strength to support the loads imposed during erection (1926.752(b)). The controlling contractor provides it (1926.752(a)). Job-site scenario: the GC hands the erector the test report and written approval before the first column is set.

test.question: Under 1926.760(a)(1), above what height must an employee doing steel erection (other than connectors and CDZ workers) be protected at an unprotected side or edge?
test.explanation: Each employee in steel erection on a surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 15 feet above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets, personal fall arrest, positioning device, or fall restraint systems. Connectors and controlled decking zone workers are covered separately (1926.760(a)(1), (a)(3)). Job-site scenario: a welder on an 18-foot beam ties off.

test.question: Under 1926.753(e)(1)(i), what must be used to perform a multiple lift?
test.explanation: A multiple lift may be performed only if a multiple lift rigging assembly is used, among other criteria (1926.753(e)(1)(i)). Employees doing multiple lift rigging need special training (1926.761(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: the raising gang uses a purpose-built multiple lift assembly for the beam pick.

test.question: When is a site-specific erection plan required under 1926.752(e)?
options: When the employer chooses, because of site conditions, to use alternate means and methods allowed by 1926.753(c)(5), 1926.757(a)(4), or 1926.757(e)(4); it must be developed by a qualified person
test.explanation: Where the employer elects alternate means and methods under the listed paragraphs because of site-specific conditions, a site-specific erection plan must be developed by a qualified person and be available at the work site (1926.752(e)). Job-site scenario: a curved roof requiring an alternative to standard column stability needs a plan from a qualified person.

test.question: What is the maximum number of members that may be hoisted in one multiple lift under 1926.753(e)(1)(ii)?
