Torch and hose control in enclosed spaces
Cadmium and other toxic filler metals

resources.title: Special Processes
resources.description: Ventilation and protection in welding, cutting, and heating

resources.title: Arc Welding and Cutting
resources.description: Electrode holders, cables, grounding, and shielding

test.question: Welding in a confined space where ventilation cannot be provided without blocking the access. What does 1926.353(b)(2) require?
options: Air line respirators per Subpart E, with an employee outside to keep communication and help in an emergency
test.explanation: Welding in a confined space requires general mechanical or local exhaust ventilation (1926.353(b)(1)). When sufficient ventilation cannot be obtained without blocking the access, employees inside must use air line respirators, and an employee outside must maintain communication and aid them in an emergency (1926.353(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a welder inside a small tank with a single manway uses a supplied-air respirator, with an attendant at the opening.

test.question: How must compressed gas cylinders be moved under 1926.350(a)?
options: By rolling them on their sides
Hoisted on a cradle, slingboard, or pallet (never by magnets or chokers), secured vertically on powered vehicles, and with regulators removed and caps on unless on a special carrier
test.explanation: Cylinders hoisted must be on a cradle, slingboard, or pallet, never by magnets or choker slings (1926.350(a)(2)). On powered vehicles they must be secured vertically (1926.350(a)(4)). Unless on a special carrier, regulators must be removed and caps put on before moving (1926.350(a)(6)). Job-site scenario: oxygen and acetylene go up to the deck in a cylinder cage, not choked with a sling.

test.question: Under 1926.351(d)(1), what must be done when electrode holders are left unattended?
options: Remove the electrodes and place or protect the holders so they cannot contact employees or conducting objects
test.explanation: When electrode holders are left unattended, the electrodes must be removed and the holders placed or protected so they cannot make electrical contact with employees or conducting objects (1926.351(d)(1)). Hot holders may not be dipped in water (1926.351(d)(2)). Job-site scenario: at break, the welder pulls the rod and hangs the stinger on an insulated hook.

test.question: During lunch, a torch is left in an enclosed space. What does 1926.352(g) require?
options: Positively shut off the gas supply to the torch outside the enclosed space; overnight and at shift changes, remove the torch and hose
test.explanation: To prevent fire from gas leaking through torch valves, the gas supply must be positively shut off outside the enclosed space whenever the torch is unattended for a substantial period, such as lunch. Overnight and at shift changes, the torch and hose must be removed (1926.352(g)). Job-site scenario: the cylinder valves are closed at the manway before the crew breaks.

test.question: Brazing with cadmium-bearing filler in an enclosed space requires what under 1926.353(c)(1)(iii)?
options: General mechanical or local exhaust ventilation meeting 1926.353(a)
test.explanation: Welding, cutting, or heating in enclosed spaces involving cadmium-bearing filler materials must be done with general mechanical or local exhaust ventilation meeting 1926.353(a) (1926.353(c)(1)(iii)). In open air, employees must use filter-type respirators (1926.353(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: silver brazing with cadmium filler in a mechanical room uses a portable fume extractor.

test.question: What does 1926.350(f) require for oxy-fuel hoses?
options: Any hose may be used for either gas
Fuel gas and oxygen hoses must be easily distinguishable and not interchangeable, and couplings must not unlock by straight pull without rotary motion
test.explanation: Fuel gas and oxygen hoses must be easily distinguishable (by color or surface feel) and not interchangeable (1926.350(f)(1)). Couplings must be a type that cannot be unlocked by a straight pull without rotary motion (1926.350(f)(5)). Flashback arrestors are good practice but are not named in 1926.350. Job-site scenario: a hose that will not pass the pull test is replaced.

test.question: During inert-gas metal-arc welding, how far must chlorinated solvents be kept from the exposed arc under 1926.353(d)(1)(i), unless shielded?
test.explanation: Chlorinated solvents must be kept at least 200 feet from the exposed arc unless shielded, and surfaces cleaned with them must be thoroughly dry before welding (1926.353(d)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the degreasing station is moved away from the MIG welding area.

test.question: Welding on a wall could pass sparks or heat to the other side. What does 1926.352(f) require?
options: Nothing; only the welding side matters
Only a fire blanket for overhead work
The same precautions on the opposite side as on the side being welded
test.explanation: When welding, cutting, or heating is done on walls, floors, or ceilings, the same precautions must be taken on the opposite side as on the welding side (1926.352(f)). Job-site scenario: a second fire watch checks the room behind the wall where a bracket is welded.

test.question: Inert-gas metal-arc welding on stainless steel requires what under 1926.353(d)(1)(iv)?
options: The requirements of 1926.353(c)(2) (local exhaust ventilation or air line respirators), to protect against nitrogen dioxide
test.explanation: When inert-gas metal-arc welding is performed on stainless steel, the requirements of 1926.353(c)(2) apply to protect against dangerous concentrations of nitrogen dioxide (1926.353(d)(1)(iv)). In enclosed spaces, (c)(2) requires local exhaust ventilation or air line respirators. Job-site scenario: MIG welding stainless handrail in a stairwell uses local exhaust at the arc.

test.question: Before heating a surface with a toxic preservative coating in an enclosed space, what does 1926.354(c)(1) require?
options: Strip the toxic coating at least 4 inches from the area of heat application, or protect employees with air line respirators
test.explanation: In enclosed spaces, surfaces with toxic preservatives must be stripped for at least 4 inches from the area of heat application, or employees must be protected by air line respirators (1926.354(c)(1)). Coatings of unknown flammability must first be tested by a competent person (1926.354(a)). Job-site scenario: the painted beam is ground back before the cut.

title: Hazardous Materials - Identification
topics: Training at initial assignment and for new hazards
Access to the written program, chemical list, and SDSs
Chemical list in the written program

resources.title: Chemical Inventory Requirement
resources.description: Written program and list of hazardous chemicals (applies to construction via 1926.59)

test.question: Which elements must appear on the label of a shipped container of a hazardous chemical under 1910.1200(f)(1)?
options: Product identifier, signal word, hazard statement(s), pictogram(s), precautionary statement(s), and the responsible party's name, U.S. address, and phone number
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Shipped containers must carry the product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and the name, U.S. address, and U.S. phone number of the responsible party (1910.1200(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: the paint thinner can shows the flame pictogram, "Danger," and hazard statements.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(g)(8), how must safety data sheets be kept?
options: For 30 years after use, in the office
In the workplace and readily accessible to employees in their work areas during each work shift (electronic access is fine if there are no barriers)
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. SDSs must be kept in the workplace and readily accessible during each shift to employees in their work areas. Electronic access is permitted if it creates no barriers to immediate access (1910.1200(g)(8)). Employees who travel between sites may have SDSs kept at the primary facility if information is immediately available in an emergency (1910.1200(g)(9)). Job-site scenario: the SDS binder is in the gang box, or the app works without a login.

test.question: When must HazCom training be given under 1910.1200(h)(1)?
options: At initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard employees have not been trained on is introduced into their work area
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Training is required at the time of initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into the work area (1910.1200(h)(1)). Job-site scenario: before the new epoxy coating system is used, the crew is trained on it.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(h)(2)(iii), employees must be informed of the location and availability of:
options: The written hazard communication program, including the required list(s) of hazardous chemicals, and the SDSs
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Employees must be informed of the location and availability of the written program, including the list(s) of hazardous chemicals, and the SDSs (1910.1200(h)(2)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the orientation shows where the HazCom binder and chemical list are kept in the trailer.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(d)(1), who must classify the hazards of chemicals?
options: Chemical manufacturers and importers (employers need not classify unless they choose not to rely on the manufacturer's or importer's classification)
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Chemical manufacturers and importers must evaluate and classify the chemicals they produce or import. Employers are not required to classify unless they choose not to rely on the manufacturer's or importer's classification (1910.1200(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the contractor relies on the supplier's classification shown on the SDS.

test.question: A worker needs to choose gloves for a new solvent. Which SDS section has exposure controls and personal protection information under 1910.1200(g)(2)?
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. SDS Section 8 is "Exposure controls/personal protection" (1910.1200(g)(2)(viii)). Job-site scenario: the foreman checks Section 8 for the recommended glove material.

test.question: A worker fills a bucket from a labeled drum and uses it right away, emptying it before leaving. Under 1910.1200(f)(8), must the bucket be labeled?
options: No; portable containers filled from labeled containers for the immediate use of the employee who did the transfer are exempt
Yes, every container must always be labeled
Only if it is larger than 5 gallons
Labeling is optional for all containers
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Workplace containers must generally be labeled (1910.1200(f)(6)), but portable containers filled from labeled containers and intended only for the immediate use of the employee who did the transfer are exempt (1910.1200(f)(8)). Job-site scenario: a cleaning solution bucket that will be used by others across shifts must be labeled.

test.question: What must the list of hazardous chemicals in the written program include under 1910.1200(e)(1)(i)?
options: The hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier that is referenced on the appropriate SDS
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. The written program must include a list of hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier referenced on the appropriate SDS. The list may cover the whole workplace or individual work areas (1910.1200(e)(1)(i)). Quantities and locations are not required by HazCom. Job-site scenario: the site list names each product as it appears on its SDS.

test.question: On a multi-employer site, what must the written HazCom program also include under 1910.1200(e)(2)?
options: Methods for giving other employers access to SDSs, informing them of precautionary measures, and informing them of the labeling system used
A list of every subcontractor's employees
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Employers whose chemicals may expose other employers' employees must include methods to give the other employers on-site access to SDSs, inform them of precautionary measures, and inform them of the labeling system (1910.1200(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: the GC's program explains how subs get SDSs for products stored in the shared conex.

test.question: Per 1910.1200 Appendix C (C.2.3.1), what must every GHS pictogram look like?
options: A yellow triangle with black text
A square set on a point, with a black hazard symbol on a white background and a red frame
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Pictograms must be a square set at a point, with a black hazard symbol on a white background and a red frame wide enough to be clearly visible (1910.1200 Appendix C (C.2.3.1)). Which symbol goes with which hazard (such as corrosion) is shown in Figure C.1, which is an image in the eCFR. Job-site scenario: the acid container label shows a red-bordered diamond pictogram.

resources.title: Fire Prevention
resources.description: Includes indoor storage and segregation of noncompatible materials

resources.title: Indoor Storage of Flammable Liquids
resources.description: Cabinet limits and indoor storage requirements

test.question: Under 1926.151(d)(3), how must noncompatible materials that may create a fire hazard be stored indoors?
options: Segregated by a barrier with a fire resistance of at least 1 hour
test.explanation: Noncompatible materials that may create a fire hazard must be segregated by a barrier with a fire resistance of at least 1 hour (1926.151(d)(3)). In general storage, noncompatible materials must be segregated (1926.250(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: oxidizers are stored behind a rated partition, away from flammable liquids.

test.question: Under 1926.152(b)(3), how much Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquid may be stored in one storage cabinet?
test.explanation: No more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, and/or 3 flammable liquids, or 120 gallons of Category 4, may be stored in any one cabinet. No more than three cabinets may be in a single storage area (1926.152(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: once the cabinet holds 60 gallons of solvents, extra product goes to an inside storage room.

test.question: What does 1926.152(a)(1) require for handling flammable liquids in quantities of 5 gallons or less?
options: Approved safety cans or DOT-approved containers (except highly viscous liquids; 1 gallon or less may stay in the original container)
test.explanation: Only approved containers and portable tanks may be used to store and handle flammable liquids. Approved safety cans or DOT-approved containers must be used for 5 gallons or less, except for highly viscous liquids, and 1 gallon or less may stay in its original container (1926.152(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: gasoline for the saws is kept in a red approved safety can.

test.question: Under 1926.152(a)(2), where may flammable liquids NOT be stored?
options: In areas used for exits, stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people
test.explanation: Flammable liquids may not be stored in areas used for exits, stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people (1926.152(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: fuel cans are moved out of the stair landing.

test.question: Under 1926.152(c)(1), outdoor storage of flammable liquid containers (60 gallons or less each) is limited to:
options: 1,100 gallons per pile, piles 5 feet apart, and no nearer than 20 feet to a building
500 gallons per pile, 10 feet from buildings
2,200 gallons per pile, touching the building
test.explanation: Outdoor storage of containers up to 60 gallons each may not exceed 1,100 gallons in any one pile, with 5-foot clearance between piles and at least 20 feet from a building (1926.152(c)(1)). A 12-foot-wide fire apparatus access way must be within 200 feet (1926.152(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: drums are staged in two piles 5 feet apart, 25 feet from the trailer.

test.question: Under 1926.152(e)(2), what is required when transferring Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids between containers?
options: The containers must be electrically interconnected (bonded)
test.explanation: Transfer of Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids from one container to another may be done only when the containers are electrically interconnected (bonded) (1926.152(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: a bonding wire connects the drum and the safety can before dispensing.

test.question: What does 1926.152(c)(3) require for outdoor flammable liquid storage areas?
options: Grading to divert spills away from buildings, or a curb or earth dike at least 12 inches high with drainage provisions
test.explanation: The storage area must be graded to divert spills away from buildings or other exposures, or be surrounded by a curb or earth dike at least 12 inches high, with provisions for draining water or spills (1926.152(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: the fuel storage pad has a 12-inch berm and a drain valve.

test.question: Under 1926.152(d)(1), where must a portable fire extinguisher be placed for a room storing more than 60 gallons of flammable liquids?
options: Inside the room at the back
Outside the room, no more than 10 feet from the door, rated at least 20-B
test.explanation: At least one portable fire extinguisher rated at least 20-B must be outside, and no more than 10 feet from, the door of any room storing more than 60 gallons of flammable liquids (1926.152(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a 20-B extinguisher hangs just outside the paint storage room door.

test.question: Under 1926.152(b)(2)(iii), how must flammable liquid storage cabinets be labeled?
options: Conspicuously, with "Flammable-Keep Away from Open Flames"
test.explanation: Cabinets must be labeled in conspicuous lettering, "Flammable-Keep Away from Open Flames" (1926.152(b)(2)(iii)). Job-site scenario: a site-built plywood cabinet gets the required label before use.

test.question: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, what does 1926.50(g) require?
options: Suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body within the work area for immediate emergency use
A phone number for poison control
test.explanation: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use (1926.50(g)). Job-site scenario: a portable eyewash station is set up next to the battery charging area.

resources.title: Respiratory Standards
resources.description: Respiratory protection standard (applies to construction via 1926.103)

resources.title: Medical Evaluation Requirements
resources.description: Medical evaluation before fit testing or respirator use

test.question: How often must an employee using a tight-fitting respirator be fit tested under 1910.134(f)(2)?
options: Before initial use, whenever a different facepiece is used, and at least annually
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Fit testing is required before initial use, whenever a different facepiece (size, style, model, or make) is used, and at least annually (1910.134(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: a laborer cutting concrete is re-fit tested every year on the same half-mask model.

test.question: Under 1910.134(e)(2)(i), how must the physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP) perform medical evaluations?
options: By a basic exam of the PLHCP's choosing
No evaluation is needed for half masks
Using a medical questionnaire, or an initial medical examination that obtains the same information
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must identify a PLHCP to perform medical evaluations using a medical questionnaire or an initial medical exam that obtains the same information (1910.134(e)(2)(i)). The evaluation must be done before fit testing or use (1910.134(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: new hires complete the Appendix C questionnaire, which a PLHCP reviews before fit testing.

test.question: When there is no end-of-service-life indicator for an organic vapor cartridge, what must the employer do under 1910.134(d)(3)(iii)(B)(2)?
options: Implement a change schedule based on objective information or data, described in the written program
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Without an appropriate ESLI, the employer must implement a canister/cartridge change schedule based on objective information or data, and describe its basis in the written program (1910.134(d)(3)(iii)(B)(2)). Job-site scenario: the painting crew changes cartridges at the interval set by the manufacturer's service-life calculator.

test.question: What must the employer do before selecting a respirator under 1910.134(d)(1)(iii)?
options: Identify and evaluate the respiratory hazards, including a reasonable estimate of exposures and the contaminant's chemical state and physical form
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must identify and evaluate workplace respiratory hazards, including a reasonable estimate of employee exposures and the contaminant's chemical state and physical form (1910.134(d)(1)(iii)). It must select a NIOSH-certified respirator (1910.134(d)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: silica monitoring results drive the choice between a half mask and a PAPR.

test.question: When must a user seal check be performed on a tight-fitting respirator under 1910.134(g)(1)(iii)?
options: Each time the respirator is put on
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Employees must perform a user seal check each time they put on a tight-fitting respirator (1910.134(g)(1)(iii)). Job-site scenario: positive and negative pressure checks are done every time the mask is donned, including after breaks.

test.question: Under 1910.134(g)(1)(i)(A), what facial hair prohibits wearing a tight-fitting respirator?
options: Facial hair that comes between the sealing surface of the facepiece and the face, or that interferes with valve function
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Tight-fitting respirators may not be worn by employees with facial hair that comes between the sealing surface and the face or interferes with valve function (1910.134(g)(1)(i)(A)). A mustache that stays clear of the seal is not prohibited by this text. Job-site scenario: a worker with a full beard switches to a loose-fitting PAPR hood.

test.question: How must respirators shared by more than one employee be cleaned under 1910.134(h)(1)(ii)?
options: Cleaned and disinfected before being worn by a different individual
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Respirators issued to more than one employee must be cleaned and disinfected before being worn by different individuals (1910.134(h)(1)(ii)), using Appendix B-2 or equivalent manufacturer procedures (1910.134(h)(1)). Job-site scenario: the shared full-face respirator is cleaned and disinfected between users.

test.question: How must respirators be stored under 1910.134(h)(2)(i)?
options: Protected from damage, contamination, dust, sunlight, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, and damaging chemicals, and stored to prevent deformation of the facepiece and exhalation valve
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Respirators must be stored to protect them from damage, contamination, dust, sunlight, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, and damaging chemicals, and packed to prevent deformation of the facepiece and exhalation valve (1910.134(h)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: the half mask goes in a sealed bag in the gang box, not loose on the dashboard.

test.question: How often must the respiratory program be evaluated under 1910.134(l)(1)?
options: As necessary to ensure the written program is being effectively implemented and remains effective
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must conduct workplace evaluations as necessary to ensure the written program is effectively implemented and continues to be effective (1910.134(l)(1)). Job-site scenario: the program administrator reviews the program when the job moves from demolition to coatings.

test.question: Under 1910.134(m)(2), how long must fit test records be kept?
options: Until the next fit test is administered
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must keep a record of each employee's qualitative and quantitative fit tests (1910.134(m)(2)(i)), retained until the next fit test is administered (1910.134(m)(2)(ii)). A written copy of the current program must also be kept (1910.134(m)(3)). Job-site scenario: last year's fit test record stays on file until this year's test is done.

title: Noise Exposure and Hearing Conservation
topics: When ear protection must be provided
Measuring on the A-scale at slow response

resources.title: Hearing Conservation Program Requirement
resources.description: Continuing hearing conservation program and combined-exposure calculation

test.question: Under Table D-2 of 1926.52, what is the permissible noise exposure for 8 hours per day?
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 90 dBA (slow response) for 8 hours per day (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a compactor operator at 92 dBA all shift exceeds the permissible exposure.

test.question: An employee works 4 hours at 95 dBA and 1 hour at 100 dBA. Using the formula in 1926.52(d)(2)(ii), does the exposure exceed the permissible level?
test.explanation: Fe = T1/L1 + T2/L2. With Table D-2 values L = 4 hours at 95 dBA and 2 hours at 100 dBA, Fe = 4/4 + 1/2 = 1.5. If Fe exceeds 1, the exposure exceeds permissible levels (1926.52(d)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: a saw operator's mixed day is over the limit even though neither period alone is.

test.question: Under 1926.101(a), when must ear protective devices be provided and used?
options: Wherever it is not feasible to reduce noise levels or durations to those in Table D-2
test.explanation: Wherever it is not feasible to reduce noise levels or exposure durations to the Table D-2 values, ear protective devices must be provided and used (1926.101(a)). Inserts must be fitted individually by competent persons (1926.101(b)). Job-site scenario: after quieter equipment and rotation, the remaining exposure is handled with fitted earplugs.

test.question: What does 1926.52(d)(1) require when sound levels exceed the values in Table D-2?
options: A continuing, effective hearing conservation program
test.explanation: In all cases where sound levels exceed Table D-2 values, a continuing, effective hearing conservation program must be administered (1926.52(d)(1)). 1926.52 does not spell out program elements such as annual audiograms; those are in the general-industry rule (1910.95). Job-site scenario: crews regularly over 90 dBA are enrolled in the company's hearing conservation program.

test.question: What does 1926.52(e) say about impulsive or impact noise?
options: It should not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level
Double hearing protection is required over 105 dB
test.explanation: Exposure to impulsive or impact noise should not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level (1926.52(e)). Note that the text says "should" (recommended under 1926.32(r)), not "shall". Job-site scenario: powder-actuated tool use is planned to keep peak exposure below 140 dB.

test.question: Under 1926.52(c), how is noise with maxima at intervals of 1 second or less treated?
test.explanation: If variations in noise level involve maxima at intervals of 1 second or less, the noise is considered continuous (1926.52(c)). Job-site scenario: a jackhammer's rapid blows are treated as continuous noise for Table D-2.

test.question: Under 1926.52(b), what must be done first when sound levels exceed Table D-2?
options: Use feasible administrative or engineering controls; if they fail to bring levels within the table, provide and use PPE
test.explanation: When sound levels exceed Table D-2, feasible administrative or engineering controls must be used. If they fail to bring levels within the table, PPE must be provided and used (1926.52(b)). Job-site scenario: an enclosure is put around the generator first; earplugs cover what remains.

test.question: Under Table D-2 of 1926.52, how long may an employee be exposed to 100 dBA per day?
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 2 hours per day at 100 dBA (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a worker running a cut-off saw at 100 dBA without controls is limited to 2 hours.

test.question: How must sound levels be measured for comparison with Table D-2 under 1926.52(a)?
options: On the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response
test.explanation: Protection is required when sound levels exceed Table D-2 as measured on the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response (1926.52(a)). Job-site scenario: the safety lead sets the meter to A-weighting, slow response, before surveying the saw cutting.

test.question: How long does Table D-2 of 1926.52 permit at 95 dBA?
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 4 hours per day at 95 dBA (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a chipping-gun operator at 95 dBA is rotated off after 4 hours unless controls reduce the level.

resources.title: Power Line Standards
resources.description: General requirements for power transmission and distribution work

resources.title: Working On or Near Exposed Energized Parts
resources.description: Qualified-employee, approach distance, arc hazard, and fuse handling rules

resources.title: PPE Requirements
resources.description: Personal protective equipment for line work

test.question: Under 1926.960(b)(1), who may work on exposed energized lines, or in areas with unguarded, uninsulated energized lines operating at 50 volts or more?
options: Any apprentice under supervision by radio
Anyone with a hard hat rated Class E
test.explanation: Only qualified employees may work on or with exposed energized lines or parts of equipment (1926.960(b)(1)(i)), or in areas containing unguarded, uninsulated energized lines or parts operating at 50 volts or more (1926.960(b)(1)(ii)). Lines are treated as energized unless deenergized under 1926.961 (1926.960(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a laborer does not enter the open vault with energized cables; the qualified lineworker does.

test.question: Under 1926.960(h), what must an employee use to install or remove fuses with a terminal energized at more than 300 volts?
options: Tools or gloves rated for the voltage
test.explanation: When installing or removing fuses with one or both terminals energized at more than 300 volts, or with exposed parts energized at more than 50 volts, the employee must use tools or gloves rated for the voltage (1926.960(h)). Job-site scenario: a hot stick rated for the circuit is used to pull the cutout fuse.

test.question: When attaching a protective ground to a line, what order does 1926.962(f)(1) require?
options: Ground-end connection first, then the other end with a live-line tool
test.explanation: The employee must attach the ground-end connection first, then attach the other end with a live-line tool. For 600 volts or less, other insulating equipment may be allowed (1926.962(f)(1)). Removal is the reverse: line end first with a live-line tool, then the ground end (1926.962(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew clamps to the ground rod first, then uses a hot stick to put the clamp on the conductor.

test.question: Under 1926.960(g)(1), what must the employer assess for employees doing line work?
options: The workplace, to identify employees exposed to hazards from flames or electric arcs
test.explanation: The employer must assess the workplace to identify employees exposed to hazards from flames or electric arcs (1926.960(g)(1)). For each exposed employee, it must make a reasonable estimate of incident heat energy (1926.960(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: the arc assessment for switching work drives the arc-rated clothing selection.

test.question: Per Table E-5 (1926.97(c)(2)(viii)), how often must rubber insulating gloves be electrically tested?
options: Before first issue and every 6 months thereafter, when insulating value is suspect, after repair, and after use without protectors
test.explanation: Electrical protective equipment must be periodically tested per Tables E-4 and E-5 (1926.97(c)(2)(viii)). Table E-5 sets rubber insulating gloves at before first issue and every 6 months thereafter, plus when insulating value is suspect, after repair, and after use without protectors. Sleeves and blankets are every 12 months. Job-site scenario: the glove tracking sheet shows test dates under 6 months old.

test.question: Under 1926.965(b), how must employees enter and exit a manhole or vault more than 4 feet deep?
options: With a ladder or other climbing device, never by stepping on cables or hangers
test.explanation: Employees must use a ladder or other climbing device to enter and exit a manhole or subsurface vault more than 4 feet deep, and may not climb in or out by stepping on cables or hangers (1926.965(b)). While work is done in a manhole with energized equipment, an employee with first-aid training must be available at the surface (1926.965(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a portable ladder is set in the vault before the splicer climbs down.

test.question: For field work by two or more employees on lines energized at 50 volts or more, how many first-aid trained persons does 1926.951(b)(1) require at the work location?
test.explanation: In addition to 1926.50, when employees work on or with exposed lines energized at 50 volts or more, field work involving two or more employees at a location needs at least two trained persons available (1926.951(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: a three-person line crew has two members with current first-aid/CPR cards.

test.question: Under 1926.952(c)(1), when work is repetitive and similar through the day, at least how many job briefings are required?
options: At least one before the start of the first job of each day or shift
Only when a supervisor is present
test.explanation: If the work during the day or shift is repetitive and similar, at least one job briefing must be held before the start of the first job of each day or shift (1926.952(c)(1)). Additional briefings are required if significant changes occur (1926.952(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: the tailboard briefing happens before the first pole change of the day.

test.question: When working within reaching distance of exposed energized parts, what does 1926.960(f) require for items like rings and watches?
options: Remove them or render them nonconductive, unless they do not increase the hazard
test.explanation: The employer must ensure the employee removes or renders nonconductive all exposed conductive articles, such as keychains, watch chains, rings, or wristwatches and bands, unless they do not increase the hazard of contact (1926.960(f)). Job-site scenario: the lineworker takes off a wedding ring before working near the energized bus.

test.question: Under 1926.964(d)(4), what must happen during adverse weather when working on towers or structures (except emergency restoration)?
options: Discontinue work when adverse weather (such as thunderstorms in the vicinity, high winds, snow or ice storms) would make the work hazardous despite the required practices
test.explanation: Except during emergency restoration, employees must discontinue work on towers and structures when adverse weather would make the work hazardous despite the required practices (1926.964(d)(4)). The note lists thunderstorms in the vicinity, high winds, snow storms, and ice storms as examples. Job-site scenario: the tower crew comes down when lightning is reported nearby.

title: Pile Driving and Site Clearing
topics: Overhead protection for pile driver operators
Rollover guards and canopies on clearing equipment

resources.title: Pile Driver General Requirements
resources.description: Overhead protection, blocking devices, and hose restraints

test.question: What overhead protection does 1926.603(a)(3) require for pile driving equipment?
options: Protection that does not obscure the operator's vision, equivalent to 2-inch planking or other solid material of equivalent strength
test.explanation: Overhead protection that will not obscure the operator's vision, and that meets Subpart N, must be provided. It must be the equivalent of 2-inch planking or other solid material of equivalent strength (1926.603(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: the pile driver cab roof is solid plate, not mesh.

test.question: Under 1926.603(a)(5), what must be placed in the leads while employees work under the hammer?
options: Nothing if the hammer is resting
A blocking device capable of safely supporting the weight of the hammer
test.explanation: A blocking device capable of safely supporting the hammer's weight must be placed in the leads under the hammer at all times while employees work under it (1926.603(a)(5)). Stop blocks must keep the hammer from being raised against the head block (1926.603(a)(4)). Job-site scenario: before changing the cushion, the crew pins the blocking device under the hammer.

test.question: How must the steam hose to a steam hammer be secured under 1926.603(a)(9)?
options: Securely attached to the hammer with an adequate length of at least 1/4-inch diameter chain or cable, to prevent whipping if the joint breaks
test.explanation: Steam hose to a steam hammer or jet pipe must be secured to the hammer with an adequate length of at least 1/4-inch chain or cable to prevent whipping if the joint breaks. Air hammer hoses need the same protection (1926.603(a)(9)). Each hose connection needs safety chains or equivalent (1926.603(a)(10)). Job-site scenario: whip checks are on every air-hammer coupling.

test.question: Under 1926.603(a)(11), what must steam line controls consist of?
options: Two shutoff valves, one of which is a quick-acting lever type within easy reach of the hammer operator
test.explanation: Steam line controls must consist of two shutoff valves, one a quick-acting lever type within easy reach of the hammer operator (1926.603(a)(11)). Job-site scenario: the operator can kill steam to the hammer with one lever pull.

test.question: Under 1926.603(c)(1), whom may pile driver engineers and winchmen accept signals from?
options: Any person who sees a problem, for all signals
test.explanation: Engineers and winchmen may accept signals only from the designated signalmen (1926.603(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: the winchman ignores waves from a passing laborer and watches the designated signalman.

test.question: What does 1926.603(c)(2) require while piling is being hoisted into the leads?
options: Workers steady the pile by hand underneath
All employees must be kept clear
Only the foreman may stay close
test.explanation: All employees must be kept clear when piling is being hoisted into the leads (1926.603(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew stands back until the pile is stabbed and set in the leads.

test.question: Piles are being driven in an excavated pit. What does 1926.603(c)(3) require for the pit walls?
options: Slope them to the angle of repose, or sheet-pile and brace them
test.explanation: When piles are driven in an excavated pit, the walls must be sloped to the angle of repose or sheet-piled and braced (1926.603(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: the pile cap pit is sheet-piled and braced before the driver works in it.

test.question: When the tops of driven piles must be cut off, what does 1926.603(c)(5) require?
options: Suspend pile driving, unless the cutting is at least twice the length of the longest pile away from the driver
test.explanation: Pile driving must be suspended when cutting off pile tops, except where the cutting is at least twice the length of the longest pile from the driver (1926.603(c)(5)). Job-site scenario: with 60-foot piles, cutoff crews work at least 120 feet from the active driver, or driving stops.

test.question: Under 1926.604(a)(1), how must employees doing site clearing be protected?
options: From the hazards of irritant and toxic plants, and suitably instructed in the first aid treatment available
test.explanation: Employees engaged in site clearing must be protected from the hazards of irritant and toxic plants and be suitably instructed in the first aid treatment available (1926.604(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: the clearing crew gets long sleeves, barrier cream, and a briefing on poison oak exposure.

test.question: What protection does 1926.604(a)(2) require on rider-operated site clearing equipment?
options: Rollover guards, plus an overhead and rear canopy guard (overhead of at least 1/8-inch steel plate or 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch, or equivalent)
test.explanation: All site clearing equipment must have rollover guards. Rider-operated equipment also needs an overhead and rear canopy guard: the overhead must be at least 1/8-inch steel plate or 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch (or equivalent), and the rear opening covered with at least 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch (1926.604(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: the dozer clearing timber has a screened canopy against falling limbs.
