resources.title: Air Quality and Monitoring
resources.description: Air monitoring requirements for underground construction

resources.title: Emergency Provisions
resources.description: Hoisting capability, self-rescuers, and rescue teams

test.question: Under 1926.800(j)(1)(ii)(A), what oxygen range must underground work area atmospheres be tested to assure?
options: At least 19.5% and no more than 22%
test.explanation: The atmosphere in all underground work areas must be tested as often as necessary to assure it contains at least 19.5% and no more than 22% oxygen (1926.800(j)(1)(ii)(A)). A competent person must perform the air monitoring (1926.800(j)(1)(i)(A)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks oxygen at the heading before the shift goes in.

test.question: When is mechanical ventilation required in underground work areas under 1926.800(k)(1)(ii)?
options: In all underground work areas, unless the employer can show natural ventilation provides the necessary air quality
test.explanation: Mechanical ventilation must be provided in all underground work areas unless the employer can demonstrate that natural ventilation provides the necessary air quality through sufficient volume and flow (1926.800(k)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the tunnel runs a vent fan and duct to the face.

test.question: What does 1926.800(c) require for tracking people underground?
options: A check-in/check-out procedure so above-ground personnel can determine an accurate count of persons underground in an emergency
test.explanation: The employer must maintain a check-in/check-out procedure so above-ground personnel can determine an accurate count of persons underground in an emergency (1926.800(c)). The procedure is not required once underground facilities designed for human occupancy are sufficiently complete that permanent environmental controls are effective and the remaining work will not cause an environmental hazard or structural failure. Job-site scenario: brass tags on a board at the shaft collar show who is below.

test.question: What emergency equipment does 1926.800(g)(2) require to be immediately available to employees underground?
options: NIOSH-approved self-rescuers at work stations where employees might be trapped by smoke or gas
test.explanation: The employer must provide NIOSH-approved self-rescuers, immediately available to all employees at underground work stations where they might be trapped by smoke or gas (1926.800(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: each miner carries or has within reach a self-rescuer at the heading.

test.question: Under 1926.800(q)(1), when must drilling equipment be inspected?
options: By a competent person prior to each use, with safety defects corrected before use
test.explanation: A competent person must inspect all drilling and associated equipment before each use, and equipment defects affecting safety must be corrected before use (1926.800(q)(1)). Haulage equipment must be inspected by a competent person before each shift (1926.800(r)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the jumbo is inspected before drilling the round.

test.question: Where are the illumination requirements for underground construction found, per 1926.800(l)(1)?
options: Table D-3 of 1926.56 (5 foot-candles for tunnels and shafts generally, 10 at the heading during drilling, mucking, and scaling)
test.explanation: Illumination requirements for underground construction are in Table D-3 of 1926.56 (1926.800(l)(1)). Table D-3 lists 5 foot-candles for tunnels, shafts, and general underground work areas, with at least 10 foot-candles at the tunnel and shaft heading during drilling, mucking, and scaling. Job-site scenario: extra lights are placed at the face during drilling.

test.question: When rapid excavation machines are used, what monitoring does 1926.800(j)(1)(iv) require?
options: A continuous flammable gas monitor operated at the face, with sensors as high and close to the cutter head as practicable
test.explanation: When rapid excavation machines are used, a continuous flammable gas monitor must be operated at the face, with sensors placed as high and close to the front of the cutter head as practicable (1926.800(j)(1)(iv)). Job-site scenario: the TBM's methane monitor runs continuously at the cutter head.

test.question: Under 1926.800(f)(1), what communication is required when natural voice communication is ineffective?
options: A power-assisted means of voice communication between the work face, the bottom of the shaft, and the surface
test.explanation: When natural unassisted voice communication is ineffective, a power-assisted means of voice communication must be used between the work face, the bottom of the shaft, and the surface (1926.800(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: a hardwired phone system connects the heading, shaft bottom, and collar.

test.question: How much fresh air must be supplied for each employee underground under 1926.800(k)(2)?
options: At least 200 cubic feet per minute
test.explanation: At least 200 cubic feet of fresh air per minute must be supplied for each employee underground (1926.800(k)(2)). Job-site scenario: with 15 workers underground, the ventilation plan delivers at least 3,000 cfm of fresh air.

test.question: Under 1926.800(o)(1), how must portal openings and access areas be protected?
options: Guarded by shoring, fencing, head walls, shotcreting, or equivalent, with adjacent areas scaled or secured against loose soil, rock, or fractured materials
test.explanation: Portal openings and access areas must be guarded by shoring, fencing, head walls, shotcreting, or equivalent protection. Adjacent areas must be scaled or secured to prevent loose soil, rock, or fractured materials from endangering the portal and access area (1926.800(o)(1)). Job-site scenario: the tunnel portal has a steel canopy and scaled face.

title: Work in Compressed Air
topics: Re-examination after absence or after 1 year
Fire watch for hot work under pressure

resources.title: Compressed Air Standards
resources.description: Work in compressed air environments (caissons, tunnels)

resources.title: Medical Attendance and Examination
resources.description: Physician, examination, and medical lock requirements

test.question: Under 1926.803(a)(1), who must be present at all times during compressed air work?
options: At least one competent person designated by and representing the employer, familiar with the subpart and responsible for full compliance
test.explanation: At least one competent person designated by and representing the employer, familiar with this subpart and responsible for full compliance, must be present at all times (1926.803(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: the caisson job always has its designated competent person on shift.

test.question: Under 1926.803(b)(2), when may an employee first enter a compressed air environment?
options: Only after being examined by the physician and reported physically qualified for the work
After one week on the job
test.explanation: No employee may enter a compressed air environment until examined by the physician and reported physically qualified (1926.803(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: new sandhogs get the physician's clearance before their first lock-in.

test.question: An employee has been absent for 10 days. Under 1926.803(b)(3), what is required before they return to compressed air work?
options: A written statement from the employee
Re-examination by the physician, with their physical condition reported
test.explanation: An employee absent from work for 10 days, or absent due to sickness or injury, may not resume work until re-examined by the physician (1926.803(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: a worker back from a two-week absence sees the physician before going back under air.

test.question: Under 1926.803(b)(4), how often must employees working continuously in compressed air be re-examined?
options: At an interval designated by the physician, not to exceed 1 year
test.explanation: After continuous employment in compressed air for a period designated by the physician, not to exceed 1 year, the employee must be re-examined (1926.803(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: long-term tunnel crews have annual physicals at most a year apart.

test.question: When must a medical lock be maintained under 1926.803(b)(9)?
options: Whenever air pressure in the working chamber is increased above normal atmosphere, in immediate working order
test.explanation: A medical lock must be established and maintained in immediate working order whenever air pressure in the working chamber is raised above normal atmosphere (1926.803(b)(9)). Job-site scenario: the medical lock is ready before the chamber is pressurized.

test.question: What does 1926.803(b)(11) require be furnished to all compressed air workers?
options: Identification badges indicating the wearer is a compressed air worker, with a permanent record of badges issued
test.explanation: Identification badges must be furnished to all employees, showing the wearer is a compressed air worker, and a permanent record of all badges issued must be kept (1926.803(b)(11)). Job-site scenario: a collapsed worker found off site is identified as a compressed air worker from the badge, prompting decompression treatment.

test.question: Under 1926.803(c)(1), what communication must be maintained during compressed air work?
options: Effective and reliable means of communication, such as bells, whistles, or telephones, at all times between listed locations
test.explanation: Effective and reliable means of communication, such as bells, whistles, or telephones, must be maintained at all times between the listed locations, including the working chamber face and the compressor plant (1926.803(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: a phone links the lock tender, the face, and the compressor house.

test.question: Under 1926.803(e)(1), what must every employee going under air pressure for the first time receive?
options: Instruction on how to avoid excessive discomfort
test.explanation: Every employee going under air pressure for the first time must be instructed on how to avoid excessive discomfort (1926.803(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: before the first lock-in, the new worker is shown how to equalize ear pressure.

test.question: How must decompression be done under 1926.803(f)(1)?
options: In accordance with the Decompression Tables in Appendix A to Subpart S
Only at the end of the week
test.explanation: Decompression to normal condition must follow the Decompression Tables in Appendix A of the subpart (1926.803(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: the lock tender follows the table time for the working pressure and shift length.

test.question: While welding or flame-cutting is done in compressed air, what does 1926.803(l)(2) require?
options: A firewatch with a fire hose or approved extinguisher standing by until the operation is completed
test.explanation: While welding or flame-cutting is done in compressed air, a firewatch with a fire hose or approved extinguisher must stand by until the operation is completed (1926.803(l)(2)). Firefighting equipment must be available at all times (1926.803(l)(1)). Job-site scenario: a firewatch with a charged hose stands by during cutting in the caisson.

title: Gases, Vapors, Fumes, Dusts, Mists, and Ventilation

resources.title: Gases, Vapors, Fumes, Dusts, and Mists
eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.55
resources.description: Current text, including Table 1 exposure limits

test.question: Under 1926.55(a)(2), how is exposure to a substance in Table 1 without a "(C)" designation measured against its limit?
options: As an 8-hour time-weighted average in any work shift, from breathing-zone samples
test.explanation: For substances whose limit is not preceded by (C), exposure determined from breathing-zone air samples may not exceed the limit as an 8-hour time-weighted average in any work shift (1926.55(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a painter's solvent exposure is sampled over the shift and compared to the TWA.

test.question: Under 1926.55(a)(1), what does a "(C)" before a limit in Table 1 mean?
options: A ceiling value that may never be exceeded (assessed as a 15-minute TWA if instantaneous monitoring is not feasible)
test.explanation: Substances with limits preceded by (C) are ceiling values: exposure may at no time exceed the limit. If instantaneous monitoring is not feasible, the ceiling is assessed as a 15-minute TWA that may not be exceeded at any time during the day (1926.55(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: short bursts of a ceiling-limited vapor during mixing are checked with a 15-minute sample.

test.question: Under 1926.55(b), what must be implemented first to meet the exposure limits?
options: Administrative or engineering controls, whenever feasible; protective equipment is used when they cannot achieve full compliance
test.explanation: Administrative or engineering controls must first be implemented whenever feasible. When they cannot achieve full compliance, protective equipment or other protective measures must keep exposures within limits (1926.55(b)). Job-site scenario: a ventilation fan is set up in the garage before respirators are considered.

test.question: What is the permissible exposure limit for carbon monoxide in Table 1 of 1926.55?
test.explanation: Table 1 to 1926.55 lists carbon monoxide at 50 ppm (55 mg/m3) as an 8-hour TWA (1926.55(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: propane heaters in an enclosed level are monitored to keep CO below 50 ppm TWA. Temporary heaters also need adequate fresh air (1926.154(a)(1)).

test.question: Under 1926.55(c), does the 1926.55 exposure table apply to asbestos?
options: Yes, it sets the asbestos limit
No; asbestos exposure is governed by 1926.1101
test.explanation: Paragraphs (a) and (b) of 1926.55 do not apply to airborne asbestos, tremolite, anthophyllite, or actinolite. 1926.1101 applies instead (1926.55(c)). Formaldehyde is likewise excluded and governed by 1910.1048 (1926.55(d)). Job-site scenario: asbestos abatement follows 1926.1101 (Week 38), not Table 1.

test.question: Under 1926.57(a), when ventilation is used as an engineering control, how must the system be installed and operated?
test.explanation: Concentrations of hazardous dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, or gases may not exceed the 1926.55(a) limits. When ventilation is used as an engineering control, the system must be installed and operated according to 1926.57 (1926.57(a)). Job-site scenario: the exhaust setup for a solvent-cleaning task is checked against 1926.57.

test.question: Under 1926.57(b), how must local exhaust ventilation be designed?
options: To prevent dispersion of contaminants in harmful concentrations, without drawing them through employees' work area
To blow contaminants toward the workers
test.explanation: Local exhaust must be designed to prevent dispersion of dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, and gases in harmful concentrations, and must not draw them through the employees' work area (1926.57(b)). Job-site scenario: the fume extractor hood is placed so the plume moves away from the welder's face, not across it.

test.question: Under 1926.57(d)(1), how long must an exhaust system run?
options: Only at the start of the task
Continually during the operations it serves, and after they stop if employees remain in the contaminated zone
test.explanation: The exhaust system must operate continually during all operations it is designed to serve. If an employee remains in the contaminated zone, it must keep running after the operation stops (1926.57(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the dust collector keeps running after cutting stops while the crew cleans up.

test.question: Under 1926.57(e), where must collected contaminants from an exhaust system be discharged?
options: Back into the work area always
To the outside atmosphere (recirculation is allowed only if it does not cause harmful exposure)
test.explanation: The air outlet of every dust separator, and the contaminants collected by an exhaust system, must discharge to the outside atmosphere. Systems returning air to the work area may be used only if accumulated concentrations do not cause harmful exposure (1926.57(e)). Job-site scenario: the negative-air duct is run out a window, not into the hallway.

test.question: What respirators does 1926.57(f)(5)(i) require for protection from abrasive-blasting dusts?
options: Only respirators approved by NIOSH under 42 CFR part 84
test.explanation: Employers must use only NIOSH-approved respirators (42 CFR part 84) to protect employees from dusts produced during abrasive blasting (1926.57(f)(5)(i)). Abrasive-blasting respirators must be worn by operators in specified situations (1926.57(f)(5)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the sandblaster wears a NIOSH-approved supplied-air blast hood.

title: Silica Exposure Control
topics: Written exposure control plan and restricting access

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.1153
resources.description: Current official text of the construction silica standard

test.question: Under 1926.1153(d)(1), what is the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica?
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed to respirable crystalline silica above 50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA (1926.1153(d)(1)). The action level is 25 µg/m3 (1926.1153(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: concrete grinding exposure is kept at or below 50 µg/m3.

test.question: When the employer is not fully following Table 1, whose exposure must it assess under 1926.1153(d)(2)(i)?
options: Each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level (25 µg/m3)
test.explanation: For tasks not on Table 1, or where Table 1 is not fully implemented, the employer must assess the exposure of each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level, using the performance or scheduled monitoring option (1926.1153(d)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: a crew cutting brick with a method not on Table 1 gets air sampling.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(d)(3)(i), what must be used first to reduce silica exposure to the PEL?
options: Engineering and work practice controls, unless not feasible
test.explanation: The employer must use engineering and work practice controls to reduce exposure to or below the PEL unless it can show they are not feasible. Where they are not sufficient, they must still be used to reduce exposure as low as feasible, supplemented by respirators (1926.1153(d)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: a wet saw or vacuum shroud comes before relying on respirators.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(h)(1)(i), which employees must be offered medical surveillance?
options: Only those above the PEL for 30 days
Each employee who will be required to use a respirator under the standard for 30 or more days per year, at no cost
test.explanation: Medical surveillance must be made available at no cost, at a reasonable time and place, to each employee who will be required to use a respirator under the standard for 30 or more days per year (1926.1153(h)(1)(i)). Periodic exams are at least every three years (1926.1153(h)(3)). Job-site scenario: a chipper who will wear a respirator more than 30 days this year is offered the exam.

test.question: What does 1926.1153(f)(1) say about dry sweeping silica dust?
options: It is not allowed where it could contribute to exposure, unless wet sweeping, HEPA vacuuming, or other low-dust methods are not feasible
It is allowed with a fan
test.explanation: Dry sweeping or dry brushing is not allowed where it could contribute to exposure unless wet sweeping, HEPA vacuuming, or other methods that minimize airborne dust are not feasible (1926.1153(f)(1)). Compressed air for cleaning is restricted too (1926.1153(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew HEPA-vacuums slurry dust instead of sweeping it.

test.question: The construction silica standard has no "regulated area" requirement. What does 1926.1153(g)(1)(iv) require instead?
options: The written exposure control plan must describe procedures to restrict access to work areas when necessary, to minimize the number of employees exposed and their exposure
test.explanation: The written exposure control plan must describe the procedures used to restrict access to work areas when necessary, to minimize the number of employees exposed and their exposure, including exposures from other employers (1926.1153(g)(1)(iv)). Regulated areas appear in the general-industry silica standard (1910.1053), not 1926.1153. Job-site scenario: the plan says other trades stay out of the cut-off saw zone.

test.question: Per Table 1 of 1926.1153(c)(1), what respiratory protection is required for an outdoor jackhammer with a continuous water spray at the point of impact?
options: None for 4 hours or less per shift; APF 10 for more than 4 hours
test.explanation: For jackhammers and handheld chipping tools used outdoors with water delivery at the point of impact, Table 1 lists no respirator for 4 hours or less per shift and APF 10 for more than 4 hours (1926.1153(c)(1) Table 1). Indoors or in enclosed areas, it is APF 10 for both. Job-site scenario: a 6-hour outdoor demo shift with water calls for an APF 10 respirator.

test.question: What does 1926.1153(i)(2)(i) require of silica training?
options: Each covered employee must be able to demonstrate knowledge of the health hazards, the specific exposure tasks, the protective measures in place, and the contents of the section, among other items
test.explanation: The employer must ensure each covered employee can demonstrate knowledge and understanding of at least: the health hazards, the specific tasks that could cause exposure, the protective measures implemented, the contents of the section, and the other listed items (1926.1153(i)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: a new mason can explain which tasks create silica dust and which controls apply.

test.question: How must silica exposure and medical surveillance records be maintained under 1926.1153(j)?
options: Maintained and made available in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1020
test.explanation: Exposure records (1926.1153(j)(1)(iii)), objective data (1926.1153(j)(2)(iii)), and medical records (1926.1153(j)(3)(iii)) must be maintained and made available in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1020. Job-site scenario: air sampling results go into the company's 1910.1020 records system.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(g)(4), what must the competent person do?
options: Make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment to implement the written exposure control plan
test.explanation: The employer must designate a competent person to make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment to implement the written exposure control plan (1926.1153(g)(4)). The plan must be reviewed at least annually (1926.1153(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks that saws have working water feeds each day.

test.question: What is the action level for airborne lead in 1926.62(b)?
options: 30 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA, without regard to respirators
test.explanation: The action level is an airborne lead concentration of 30 µg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour period, without regard to respirator use (1926.62(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: a paint-removal crew sampled at 35 µg/m3 is above the action level.

test.question: Under 1926.62(j)(1)(ii), which employees must be covered by the full medical surveillance program under paragraphs (j)(2) and (j)(3)?
options: Only employees who ask to be included
Employees who are or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 30 days in any consecutive 12 months
test.explanation: A medical surveillance program under (j)(2) and (j)(3) is required for employees who are or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 30 days in any consecutive 12 months (1926.62(j)(1)(ii)). Initial medical surveillance applies on any day at or above the action level (1926.62(j)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a bridge-painting crew exposed above 30 µg/m3 for 40 days this year gets blood lead testing.

test.question: Under 1926.62(f)(1), when must respirators be used?
options: During periods when exposure exceeds the PEL, when engineering and work practice controls are insufficient, when an employee requests a respirator, and in the other listed situations
test.explanation: Respirators must be used during periods when exposure exceeds the PEL (1926.62(f)(1)(i)), during operations where engineering and work practice controls are not sufficient (1926.62(f)(1)(ii)), during periods when an employee requests a respirator (1926.62(f)(1)(iii)), and in the other listed cases. Job-site scenario: abrasive blasting of lead paint above the PEL requires respirators while controls are installed.

test.question: Under 1926.62(d)(6)(iii), how often must monitoring be repeated if exposure is above the PEL?
options: Quarterly, until two consecutive measurements at least 7 days apart are at or below the PEL (then every 6 months if at or above the action level)
test.explanation: If exposure is above the PEL, monitoring must be quarterly until at least two consecutive measurements, at least 7 days apart, are at or below the PEL (1926.62(d)(6)(iii)). Between the action level and the PEL, monitoring is at least every 6 months (1926.62(d)(6)(ii)). Job-site scenario: a crew at 70 µg/m3 is resampled every quarter.

test.question: What hygiene facilities does 1926.62(i) require for employees exposed above the PEL?
options: Clean change areas, shower facilities where feasible, and lunchroom or eating areas
test.explanation: For employees whose airborne exposure is above the PEL, the employer must provide clean change areas (1926.62(i)(2)(i)), showers where feasible (1926.62(i)(3)(i)), and lunchroom or eating facilities (1926.62(i)(4)(i)). Where showers are not provided, employees must wash hands and face at the end of the shift. Job-site scenario: a decon trailer with a change room and shower is set up for the abatement crew.

test.question: Under 1926.62(k)(1)(i), when must an employee be temporarily removed from lead exposure at or above the action level?
options: After any exposure above the PEL
When a periodic and a follow-up blood test both show a blood lead level at or above 50 µg/dl
test.explanation: The employer must remove an employee from work with exposure at or above the action level each time a periodic and a follow-up blood test both show a blood lead level at or above 50 µg/dl (1926.62(k)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a painter with two results above 50 µg/dl is reassigned away from lead exposure, with removal protection.

test.question: How must floors and surfaces with lead accumulations be cleaned under 1926.62(h)?
options: By vacuuming or other low-dust methods where possible, with HEPA vacuums; sweeping only if vacuuming has been tried and found ineffective; no compressed air unless used with a capturing ventilation system
test.explanation: Clean-up must use vacuuming or other methods that minimize airborne lead wherever possible (1926.62(h)(2)). Shoveling and dry or wet sweeping are allowed only where vacuuming has been tried and found ineffective (1926.62(h)(3)). Vacuums must have HEPA filters (1926.62(h)(4)), and compressed air may not be used unless paired with capturing ventilation (1926.62(h)(5)). Job-site scenario: paint chips are HEPA-vacuumed off the deck.

test.question: Under 1926.62(l)(1), when must lead training be given?
options: Before job assignment, and at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day
test.explanation: Training must be given before job assignment (1926.62(l)(1)(iii)) and at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day (1926.62(l)(1)(iv)). Job-site scenario: returning abatement workers get annual lead training.

test.question: What do the required warning signs say under 1926.62(m)(1)(i), and where are they posted?
options: "DANGER / LEAD WORK AREA / MAY DAMAGE FERTILITY OR THE UNBORN CHILD / CAUSES DAMAGE TO THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM / DO NOT EAT, DRINK OR SMOKE IN THIS AREA", in each work area where exposure is above the PEL
test.explanation: Warning signs with that legend must be posted in each work area where exposure is above the PEL (1926.62(m)(1)(i)). Before June 1, 2016, the older "WARNING / LEAD WORK AREA / POISON / NO SMOKING OR EATING" legend was allowed (1926.62(m)(1)(v)). Job-site scenario: the containment entrance on the bridge has the DANGER lead sign.

test.question: Under 1926.62(c)(1), what is the permissible exposure limit for lead?
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed to lead above 50 µg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour period (1926.62(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: monitoring shows 45 µg/m3, which is above the action level but within the PEL.

title: Asbestos Awareness
topics: Identifying ACM and PACM before work

test.question: Under 1926.1101(k)(3)(i), what must employers do before work begins in areas containing ACM or PACM?
options: Identify the presence, location, and quantity of ACM and/or PACM
test.explanation: Before work in areas containing ACM and PACM begins, employers must identify the presence, location, and quantity of ACM and/or PACM (1926.1101(k)(3)(i)). Thermal system insulation and surfacing material in buildings constructed no later than 1980 is presumed asbestos-containing (PACM) unless rebutted (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: before demolishing a 1970s ceiling, the GC confirms whether the spray-on fireproofing has been tested.

test.question: What are the asbestos exposure limits in 1926.1101(c)?
options: 0.1 f/cc as an 8-hour TWA, and 1.0 f/cc averaged over 30 minutes (excursion limit)
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed above 0.1 fiber per cubic centimeter as an 8-hour TWA (1926.1101(c)(1)), or above 1.0 f/cc averaged over a 30-minute sampling period (1926.1101(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: monitoring during pipe insulation removal is compared to both limits.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(b), what is Class I asbestos work?
options: Removal of thermal system insulation (TSI) and surfacing ACM and PACM
test.explanation: Class I asbestos work means removal of TSI and surfacing ACM and PACM (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Class II is removal of other ACM, such as wallboard, floor tile, and roofing. Job-site scenario: stripping pipe lagging in a boiler room is Class I.

test.question: What does 1926.1101(g)(1)(ii) require to control exposure during asbestos handling and removal?
options: Wet methods or wetting agents, except where shown infeasible
test.explanation: Wet methods or wetting agents must be used to control exposure during handling, mixing, removal, cutting, application, and cleanup, unless the employer shows wet methods are infeasible (1926.1101(g)(1)(ii)). Amended water is water with a surfactant added to penetrate ACM (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: floor tile is misted with amended water before removal.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(h)(1), which work always requires respirators?
options: Class I asbestos work (among other listed situations, such as Class II work when ACM is not removed substantially intact)
test.explanation: Respirators are required during all Class I work (1926.1101(h)(1)(i)), during Class II work when ACM is not removed in a substantially intact state (1926.1101(h)(1)(ii)), and in other listed situations. Job-site scenario: the TSI removal crew wears respirators regardless of monitoring results.

test.question: How must asbestos-contaminated waste and debris be disposed of under 1926.1101(g)(1)(iii)?
options: Promptly, in leak-tight containers (except in roofing operations covered elsewhere)
test.explanation: Wastes and debris contaminated with asbestos must be promptly cleaned up and disposed of in leak-tight containers, except in roofing operations under (g)(8)(ii) (1926.1101(g)(1)(iii)). Job-site scenario: bagged debris is sealed and labeled before leaving the regulated area.

test.question: For Class I jobs involving over 25 linear or 10 square feet of TSI or surfacing ACM/PACM, what decontamination area does 1926.1101(j)(1)(i) require?
options: An equipment room, shower area, and clean room in series, adjacent and connected to the regulated area
test.explanation: A decontamination area adjacent and connected to the regulated area is required, consisting of an equipment room, shower area, and clean room in series (1926.1101(j)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the three-stage decon unit is built at the containment entrance.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(e)(6), who must supervise asbestos work in regulated areas?
options: A competent person as defined in 1926.1101(b)
test.explanation: All asbestos work in regulated areas must be supervised by a competent person as defined in paragraph (b) (1926.1101(e)(6)). All Class I, II, and III work must be done within regulated areas (1926.1101(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: the abatement contractor's trained competent person is on site during removal.

test.question: What must regulated-area warning signs say under 1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(A)?
options: "DANGER / ASBESTOS / MAY CAUSE CANCER / CAUSES DAMAGE TO LUNGS / AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY"
test.explanation: Warning signs demarcating the regulated area must bear: DANGER / ASBESTOS / MAY CAUSE CANCER / CAUSES DAMAGE TO LUNGS / AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY (1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(A)). Where respirators and protective clothing are required, the signs must also say so (1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(B)). Job-site scenario: signs are posted far enough out to read before entering.

test.question: How long must asbestos medical surveillance records be kept under 1926.1101(n)(3)(iii)?
options: For the duration of employment plus 30 years, per 1910.1020
test.explanation: Medical surveillance records must be kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years, in accordance with 1910.1020 (1926.1101(n)(3)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the abatement firm keeps workers' medical records long after they leave.

resources.title: Evacuation Plans and Procedures eTool
resources.description: OSHA eTool for emergency action and evacuation planning

test.question: Which is one of the minimum elements of an emergency action plan under 1926.35(b)?
options: A list of equipment serial numbers
The preferred means of reporting fires and other emergencies
test.explanation: Minimum elements include escape procedures and route assignments, procedures for employees who stay to run critical operations, procedures to account for all employees after evacuation, rescue and medical duties, the preferred means of reporting emergencies, and contacts for more information (1926.35(b)(1)-(6)). Job-site scenario: the plan says to report fires by air horn and radio call to the site office.

test.question: Under 1926.35(e)(2), when must the employer review the plan with each covered employee?
options: When the plan is developed, whenever the employee's responsibilities or designated actions change, and whenever the plan changes
test.explanation: The employer must review the plan with each covered employee initially when the plan is developed, whenever the employee's responsibilities or actions under the plan change, and whenever the plan changes (1926.35(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: when a new fuel storage area changes the escape route, the crew is re-briefed.

test.question: Under 1926.35(e)(1), what must happen before the plan is implemented?
options: The employer must designate and train enough persons to assist in safe and orderly evacuation
test.explanation: Before implementing the plan, the employer must designate and train a sufficient number of persons to assist in the safe and orderly emergency evacuation of employees (1926.35(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: floor wardens are trained on each level of the high-rise job.

test.question: If the employee alarm system is used for more than one purpose, what does 1926.35(c)(2) require?
options: A distinctive signal for each purpose
test.explanation: If the alarm system is used to alert fire brigade members or for other purposes, a distinctive signal must be used for each purpose (1926.35(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: evacuation is a continuous horn; tornado shelter is three short blasts.

test.question: What must the emergency action plan establish under 1926.35(d)?
options: The types of evacuation to be used in emergency circumstances
test.explanation: The employer must establish in the plan the types of evacuation to be used in emergencies (1926.35(d)). Job-site scenario: the plan distinguishes full-site evacuation for fire from partial evacuation for a gas leak in one area.

test.question: Under 1926.35(b)(6), whom must the plan identify?
options: Names or regular job titles of persons or departments who can be contacted for more information or explanation of duties under the plan
test.explanation: The plan must include the names or regular job titles of persons or departments who can be contacted for more information or explanation of duties under the plan (1926.35(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: the plan lists the site safety manager's title and phone.

test.question: Under 1926.35(a), when must an emergency action plan be in writing?
options: When required by a particular OSHA standard; it must be written except that employers with 10 or fewer employees may communicate it orally
test.explanation: Section 1926.35 applies to emergency action plans required by a particular OSHA standard. The plan must be in writing, except as provided in the last sentence of (e)(3) for employers with 10 or fewer employees (1926.35(a)). Job-site scenario: a 40-person job site under a standard requiring an EAP keeps a written plan in the trailer.

test.question: What does 1926.35(b)(3) require the plan to include?
options: Procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed
test.explanation: The plan must include procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed (1926.35(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: foremen bring their daily sign-in sheets to the muster point.

test.question: Under 1926.50(e), what must be provided for an injured person?
options: Proper equipment for prompt transportation to a physician or hospital, or a communication system for contacting ambulance service
test.explanation: Proper equipment for prompt transportation of the injured person to a physician or hospital, or a communication system for contacting ambulance service, must be provided (1926.50(e)). Job-site scenario: a remote site keeps a vehicle and a satellite phone available for emergencies.

test.question: Under 1926.150(a)(2)-(3), what is required of firefighting equipment?
options: It may be stored in a locked trailer
Only the foreman needs to know where it is
Access to it must be maintained at all times, and it must be conspicuously located
test.explanation: Access to all available firefighting equipment must be maintained at all times (1926.150(a)(2)), and employer-provided firefighting equipment must be conspicuously located (1926.150(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: extinguishers are not blocked by material deliveries and are marked with signs.

title: Ionizing and Nonionizing Radiation
topics: Competent persons for radioactive materials and X-rays
Laser warning placards and beam control

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.54
resources.description: Current official text of the nonionizing radiation standard

test.question: Under 1926.53(a), which standards apply to construction activities using sources of ionizing radiation?
options: The pertinent provisions of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Standards for Protection Against Radiation (10 CFR part 20)
test.explanation: In construction activities using sources of ionizing radiation, the pertinent NRC provisions (10 CFR part 20) on occupational radiation exposure apply (1926.53(a)). Job-site scenario: a radiography subcontractor X-raying pipe welds works under its NRC or agreement-state license rules.

test.question: Under 1926.53(b), who may perform activities involving radioactive materials or X-rays?
options: Competent persons specially trained in the proper and safe operation of the equipment
test.explanation: Any activity involving radioactive materials or X-rays, licensed or not, must be performed by competent persons specially trained in the proper and safe operation of the equipment (1926.53(b)). Job-site scenario: only the certified radiographer operates the source camera; other trades stay out of the barricaded area.

test.question: Under 1926.54(a)-(b), who may install, adjust, and operate laser equipment?
options: Only qualified and trained employees, who must carry proof of qualification at all times
test.explanation: Only qualified and trained employees may install, adjust, and operate laser equipment (1926.54(a)), and proof of the operator's qualification must be available and in the operator's possession at all times (1926.54(b)). Job-site scenario: the laser-level operator carries their qualification card.

test.question: Above what potential exposure to direct or reflected laser light does 1926.54(c) require antilaser eye protection?
test.explanation: Employees working where potential exposure to direct or reflected laser light exceeds 0.005 watts (5 milliwatts) must be provided antilaser eye protection as specified in Subpart E (1926.54(c)). Job-site scenario: crews near a high-power alignment laser get wavelength-rated goggles.

test.question: What does 1926.54(d)-(e) require in laser work areas?
options: Standard laser warning placards posted, and beam shutters or caps used (or the laser turned off) when transmission is not needed; turned off when left unattended for substantial periods
test.explanation: Areas where lasers are used must be posted with standard laser warning placards (1926.54(d)). Beam shutters or caps must be used, or the laser turned off, when transmission is not needed, and the laser must be turned off when left unattended for a substantial period such as lunch, overnight, or shift change (1926.54(e)). Job-site scenario: the pipe laser is capped during the lunch break.

test.question: Under 1926.54(g), may a laser beam be directed at employees?
test.explanation: The laser beam shall not be directed at employees (1926.54(g)). Job-site scenario: the rotating laser is set above head height (1926.54(k) recommends this when possible).

test.question: What does 1926.54(h) require when it is raining, snowing, dusty, or foggy?
options: Laser operation must be prohibited where practicable, and in any event employees must be kept out of range of the source and target area
test.explanation: When it is raining or snowing, or there is dust or fog in the air, laser operation must be prohibited where practicable. In any event, employees must be kept out of range of the source and target area during such weather (1926.54(h)). Job-site scenario: the survey laser is shut down in dense fog.

test.question: Under 1926.54(i), what label must laser equipment bear?
test.explanation: Laser equipment must bear a label indicating its maximum output (1926.54(i)). Job-site scenario: before use, the operator checks the output label to choose eye protection.

test.question: Under 1926.54(l), employees may not be exposed to microwave power densities above:
test.explanation: Employees may not be exposed to microwave power densities in excess of 10 milliwatts per square centimeter (1926.54(l)). Job-site scenario: riggers on a telecom tower stay out of the antenna's near field while it is transmitting.

test.question: Under 1926.54(j)(1), employees may not be exposed to direct-staring laser light intensities above:
test.explanation: Employees may not be exposed to light intensities above 1 microwatt/cm2 for direct staring (1926.54(j)(1)), 1 milliwatt/cm2 for incidental observing (1926.54(j)(2)), or 2.5 watts/cm2 for diffused reflected light (1926.54(j)(3)). Job-site scenario: no one looks into the beam path of the alignment laser.
